speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Hon. L. S. ST. LAURENT (Acting Secretary of State for External Affairs): In reply to a question from the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) on October 11, I stated that the Canadian government had accepted the invitation to be represented at the conference which will meet in London on November 1 to consider the establishment of an educational and cultural organization of the united nations. I am now in a position to announce the composition of the Canadian delegation. The delegation will consist of the Right Hon. Vincent Massey, High Commissioner for Canada in London, as chairman, with Principal R. C. Wallace of Queen's University and Mr. Edmond Turcotte of Montreal as delegates. Since Mr. Massey will not be able to attend the opening sessions of the conference, Principal Wallace will act as alternate chairman of the delegation.

Export Credits
The advisers to the delegation will be Mr. T. W. L. MacDermot of the Department of External Affairs; Dr. J. G. Malloch, senior liaison officer of the National Research Council in the United Kingdom, and Dr. J. E. Robbins, of the Dominion Bureau of Statistics.
I mentioned to the house on October 11 that this conference will be mainly concerned with considering a draft constitution for the proposed organization, and this has been borne in mind in determining the composition of the Canadian delegation. If' the conference succeeds in its objects and a new international ' agency is set up under the auspices of the economic and social council of the united nations, I have no doubt that consideration will be given by the government to the development of means for ensuring that the Canadian share in the activities of the organization are carried out in close consultation with the provincial departments of education and with the associations and institutions in Canada that are concerned with educational, cultural and scientific activities.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: On the orders of the day:

maintopic: REFERENCE TO SERVICES RENDERED BY RIGHT HON. VINCENT AND MRS. MASSEY TO MEMBERS OF CANADIAN ARMED FORCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am not quite sure that the subject with which I wish to deal for a moment is quite within the rules of the house, but I would ask your indulgence with the permission of the house. It arises out of the statement that was made a moment ago by the Minister of Justice in regard to the appointment of a chairman of the Canadian delegation to the cultural and educational conference of the united nations which is shortly to meet in London. The time would seem to be opportune to express through this parliament the appreciation of the people of Canada of the invaluable services rendered by the Right Hon. Vincent and Mrs. Massey to members of our armed forces during their stay in England. We particularly desire to commend them for the leading part they played in establishing the Beaver club for other ranks of the three services and an officers' club in London, where Mrs. Massey personally helped to serve meals d-aily, as well as for their initiative in taking over a large house in Herefordshire which they converted into a convalescent home and maintained at their own expense and where many of our wounded were restored to health.
In their eagerness to promote the social welfare of our men, they have been completely and heroically forgetful of themselves and their
own anxieties We desire to extend to Mr. and Mrs. Massey our grateful thanks for the personal contribution they have made to the happiness and well-being of our men overseas during these six trying years of war.

maintopic: EXPORT CREDITS INSURANCE
subtopic: LOAN AGREEMENTS FOR PURCHASES OF CANADIAN GOODS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to make an announcement regarding credit agreements which have been concluded under the Export Credits Insurance Act. These agreements have been entered into by the Minister of Finance under part II of the act, on behalf of the governor in council upon the joint recommendation of the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Trade and Commerce.
At noon to-day a loan agreement was signed with the Belgian government. The amount of the loan is $25 million, and it is to be used for the purchase of Canadian-produced goods. The credit is repayable in thirty annual instalments, commencing in 1947. This credit will bear interest at three per cent.
As hon. members will recall, the authority of the governor in council to make loans to foreign governments under the terms of the Export Credits Insurance Act was limited to $100 million. The Belgian loan to which I have just referred exhausts the lending authority of the government. At a later date the Minister of Finance will request the house materially to increase our lending capacity under the act, and full details of the lending programme will be available at that time.
Meanwhile, I thought that the house would appreciate knowing in a general way what has been done under the act of 1944. During the first half of this year, credit agreements were entered into with Czechoslovakia and the Netherlands. The amounts and terms of these loans were made public at the time. Loan agreements have more recently been made with the Netherlands, Netherlands Indies, Norway, and a small loan has been made to the U.S.S.R. I have arranged the details of these loans in simplified tabular form, as follows:

at which the dominion government itself can borrow for a term equal to the average term of the loan plus a small margin to cover overhead costs of borrowing in addition to the interest charges. The government is following this pattern as a policy in making loans to allied nations for reconstruction purposes. As a consequence the interest rate depends upon the average length of the loan.
In addition to the loans which I have just announced, the government has agreed with certain foreign governments to increase the size of the loans and to enter into loan contracts with other governments, if the necessary legislative authority is obtained from this house allowing us to do so. Norway, Belgium, the Netherlands, and the Netherlands Indies, all wish to purchase goods which are available in Canada, greatly in excess of the amounts which so far the government has been able to make available to them for this purpose. The comparatively small loan to the U.S.S.R. was made to cover a specific group of purchases, and consideration is being given to future and larger credits.
France wishes to make large purchases to assist her in her very difficult problems of reconstruction. If the necessary authority can be obtained, the government would be prepared to negotiate a loan with France to enable her to purchase Canadian goods to a value of nearly $250 million in addition to those goods which she is able to purchase for cash.
Discussions regarding a credit have also been held with representatives of the government of China. As yet there has not been an opportunity to complete negotiations regarding the terms of this credit, but I would hope that in this case, as well as in the case of the other countries I have mentioned, it would be possible to give the house further information before it is asked to approve an increase in the amount which may be loaned.
A condition attached to all these loans is, as hon. members will recall, that the proceeds of the loans shall be used in the purchase of Canadian produced goods.
It has not been found advisable, except in one case, to include in the loan agreements specific schedules of goods to be purchased with the proceeds of the loans. In a general way the amount of the loans has been related in each case to considerations of the probable availability of the goods which our allies desire to purchase from us. But it is to the advantage of both the buyer and the seller to have a certain amount of elasticity in these large purchasing programmes. From the buyers' point of view considerations of price,

supply, delivery dates, and many other factors which may change from time to time, make it undesirable to commit them to specific programmes of purchases too far in advance. And from our own point of view, it has not been thought advisable or even possible, to make firm commitments to supply large quantities of goods-for example, wheat-up, to say, the end of 1946.
From a study of the proposed purchasing programmes it is clear that the goods which will be required will be mainly foodstuffs, raw materials, and equipment for the reconstruction and rehabilitation of transportation and communication systems. These loans may in a very real sense be called reconstruction loans. We in Canada have a very real interest in the reconstruction efforts of our war-time allies, not alone on business, but also on humanitarian grounds. Only as the economic wounds of war are healed shall we return gradually to a healthy world, the life-blood of which, as Canadians are among the first to realize, is a strong and vigorous international trade.

speechtext:
On September 14, 1945, a report was -received from the district resident architect at Victoria, B.C., in which he stated that the public building at Whitehorse was far too small and congested for the proper carrying out of the work of the Post Office Department, and recommended that a new public building be erected to take care of the Post Office Department, National Revenue Department (customs division), court house, unemployment insurance commission, R.C.M.Police, and other dominion government departments in that district.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Hon. J. L. ILSLEY (Minister of Finance) moved that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to present a measure to incorporate the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation for the purpose of (a)

Housing Act
acting in the place of the Minister of Finance in the operation of the National Housing Act, 1944, and (b) providing discounting facilities for loan and mortgage companies; to provide for the appointment and salaries of the officers and staff of the corporation and the appointment and fees of the directors; to authorize the payment out of the consolidated revenue fund of sums not exceeding twenty-five million dollars ($25,000,000) for the provision of paid-up capital for the corporation; to make available for the housing functions of the corporation moneys appropriated under the National Housing Act, 1944; and to make provisions with respect to the functions and powers of the corporation.
He said: Mr. Speaker, as stated in the resolution, the purpose of this legislation is to create a Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation which will, first, act in place of, or on behalf of the Minister of Finance in the operation of the National Housing Act; second, provide discounting facilities for the loan and mortgage companies.
To illustrate the reasons for the proposed change in the form of administration of the housing act, let me summarize briefly the kind of operations authorized by the act. First, the government is authorized to make loans for house construction purposes. Some of these are joint loans (the government's share being 25 per cent) made through private lending institutions. Some are direct government advances up to 90 per cent of the value of a low rental project. All are secured by mortgage. Second, the government is authorized to take a share of losses incurred on joint housing loans and to provide minimum guarantees to life insurance companies on housing investments approved by the minister. A third type of operation is the authority to enter into contracts for the production of new types of building materials and components. Then there are the grants for slum clearance purposes. Finally, there is authority to engage in a wide variety of promotional and research activities associated with housing, community planning, et cetera.
It will be noted that apart from promotion and research, these operations are of a commercial or quasi-commercial character. Under the National Housing Act, the government is in business

principally in the business of lending money on long term for the construction of houses. Bargaining and negotiation are involved. Risks have to be appraised.
* Questions of litigation arise from time to time. If sound investments are to be made, those responsible for the administration of the act require a background of commercial knowledge and an intimate day by day contact with development in mortgage lending throughout 47696-94i
the country. Quite obviously a minister of the crown cannot carry on the administration personally, yet the National Housing Act requires the Minister of Finance to make every important decision and to sign his name to innumerable assignments, releases and other documents relating to the mortgaged properties.
During war years, when housing activity was limited, there was no particular occasion for making a change in the form of administration, but with the end of the war and the coming into effect of the far-reaching 1944 legislation the advantages of transferring administrative responsibility from the minister to a government-owned corporation are becoming more evident. The government has therefore decided to recommend that the pattern laid down for the administration of its other lending activities through such corporations as the Canadian farm loan board, the Bank of Canada and the industrial development bank, be followed in the case of housing finance. As I shall outline later, Canada is just at the beginning of a very large, possibly an unprecedentedly large, housing programme. To deal with the greatly increased volume of housing loans and to carry out the other purposes of the housing legislation, it would have been necessary in any case greatly to enlarge the housing administration. The present time is therefore a unique occasion on which to give the administration the form which will enable it to carry out its functions most effectively.
In general, and I think rightly so, parliament has been reluctant to transfer authority from a responsible minister to a corporation, but in this case the National Housing Act lays down clearly the limits within which the administration may act and requires the approval of the governor in council on the most important matters of general policy. It will also be provided in the bill that the governor in council shall approve the by-laws of the corporation.
The corporation will take over the administration of the housing act in full except for one item, namely, grants for slum clearance. In this case, since it is a grant and not an investment, the corporation will do the preliminary work of investigation, but the Minister of Finance, with the approval of the governor in council, will retain authority to make grants directly out of the housing act appropriation.
Rediscounting facilities. The second function of the proposed corporation is to provide a supplementary source of credit for the loan and trust companies to which they can turn in time of need. In some respects, therefore,
Housing Act

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
the corporation will provide for these lending institutions the kind of rediscount facilities made available by a central bank for the ordinary commercial banks. Because the trust and loan companies are for the most part in a highly liquid position, these facilities may not be extensively used in the immediate future, but the knowledge that they are available will give the private institutions confidence and thus enable them to meet more effectively the borrowing needs of the public. In establishing these mortgage discounting facilities now, the government has in mind particularly the desirability of maintaining an adequate flow of mortgage loans in all parts of the country and of working steadily in the' direction of lower rates and more suitable terms on all kinds of mortgage lending, both rural and urban.
It will be apparent from this brief description that the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation will revive some of the functions of the central mortgage bank which, because of the war, remained dormant and will now be dissolved. In many respects, however, the facilities are on a simpler basis, the highly unsound and top heavy situation in farm mortgages which was the immediate occasion for the formation of the central mortgage bank in 1939 having been largely corrected during the intervening six years of rising farm incomes. The corporation will be empowered to buy mortgages from the lending companies and to resell them; to lend to loan and trust companies on the security of mortgages and to buy their debentures.
The capital of the corporation has been fixed at $25 million, subscribed by the Minister of Finance. About $12 million will be invested in joint housing loans now outstanding in the name of the Minister of Finance. As supplementary funds are required they will be advanced by the minister out of funds appropriated by the National Housing acts at suitable rates of interest, the intention being that there should be a margin between the rates charged by the minister and the rates charged by the corporation sufficient to cover operating expenses.
Since the corporation acts in place of the Minister of Finance uqder the National Housing Act, losses on housing loans or under any guarantee or contract will be met out of moneys appropriated under the act, leaving operating expenses and any losses in connection with the mortgage discounting business to be met by the corporation out of its own earnings. The profits of the corporation after

the establishment of a reserve fund of $5 million will be paid over annually to the Receiver General.
The success of the corporation, both in administering the National Housing Act and as a supplementary source of credit for lending institutions, will depend in large part upon having access to sound advice from all parts of the country. It is therefore, proposed that the board of directors should include five directors, one from, each of the main regions of Canada, in addition to the two executive officers, and directors representing the departments of Finance and Reconstruction and the Bank of Canada.
These are the general principles of the legislation which this resolution seeks to introduce. At a later stage when the bill, has been read, there will be an opportunity to deal with the provisions in detail.
Since the two resolutions on the order paper relate to the only housing legislation which the government intends to introduce during the present session, I think that I should at this time, in view of the very great interest in the subject both within this house and in the country at large, make a few general observations on the housing problem and on the measures which the government is taking to deal with it.
May I say at the outset that in my view, and in the view of the government as a whole, there is no problem before the country to-day more important than the provision of additional housing accommodation, particularly for those who have served with the armed forces and who are now returning to civilian life. Nor, may I add, is there any problem w'hich presents so many practical difficulties in reaching a speedy and satisfactory solution.
In this Canada is not alone. Fortunately we have been spared the destruction wrought by enemy bombs and shellfire. But in countries as immune from enemy attack as the United States and' Australia, to mention only two, are to be found much the same conditions of over-crowding and congestion, much the same shortages of labour and building materials, much the same symptoms of high construction costs, as we in Canada are struggling to cope with at the present time. I venture to say that in all countries that have taken an active part in the war will be found a greater or less degree of housing shortage and for very much the same reasons. I venture to say alar>
that no government in this or any other major belligerent country, no matter what preparations it had made in advance, could have come out of the war with sufficient accommodation to house its population in a satisfactory manner.

Housing Act
I say this to suggest that the problem should be viewed in its proper perspective as, in a very large degree at least, an inevitable consequence of the fact that for nearly six years we, like other belligerents, had to put other and more vital considerations ahead of the provision of housing.
It should be recognized, too, that the end of the war, though it released men and materials for house building, actually intensified rather than relieved the'congestion, for it meant the early return to civilian life of hundreds of thousands of soldiers, sailors, and airmen, many of whom had married wdiile overseas, intended to get married immediately or were returning to their wives and families. To illustrate the impact of demobilization on the available supply of housing, I may say in this connection that, on the basis of recent confidential surveys by the Department of National Defence, a very substantial proportion, around 40 per cent, of the married army personnel are likely to be seeking separate accommodation for their families.
. Well in advance of VE-day the government made preparatipns to speed the construction of houses. As my colleague, the Minister of Reconstruction, indicated the other day, a surprisingly large number of houses had been built during each of the years 1943 and 1944, probably more than in any of the previous thirteen or fourteen years. But it was expedient to set our sights high and the goal was fixed in the first instance at 35,000 new dwelling units for the calendar year 1945 and then at 50,000 for the first full construction year following VE-day, almost as many as had been built in any previous year in Canada.
This goal of 50.000 new dwelling units was fixed not by reference to the number of new dwellings required-from that point of view it was far short of the mark-but rather in terms of the probable supply of materials and labour over the twelve month period. It was estimated that, with the necessary cooperation from labour and industry, it would be possible to get sufficient material and labour for 50,000 houses within that period.
There is reason to believe that this goal will be substantially attained. From the evidence now available it is clear that a large house-building programme is under way. For example, in the Toronto area nearly 2,500 dwelling units were in course of construction when the labour department made its survey in midsummer. To give a few other examples: In the Montreal area over 3,200 dwelling units were under way, in the Vancouver area over 2,200 and in the Edmonton
area over 1,300. These were the numbers in course of construction at the time of the survey. Many more had been completed before the survey began and others were started after the survey was completed.
We hear many complaints these days about the difficulties being experienced by builders in obtaining certain scarce materials. I do not doubt for a moment that these complaints are in many instances well founded. But the basic reason is not that the production of building materials is at a low level. Output of most of the principal items considerably exceeds pre-war levels. Rather the difficulties stem from the fact, which I have already mentioned, that the demand for houses far exceeds even the increased supply of building materials. Since early summer the interdepartmental housing committee, which coordinates the activities of the various departments concerned with housing, has had the building materials situation under close review, and I have with me a few figures prepared by the wartime prices and trade board on present and projected production of certain relatively scarce items which indicate the steady improvement in output now taking place. Here are a few of the items that have been difficult to obtain. Output of bathtubs will probably be 12,000 units in the final quarter of 1945 and 14,000 in the first quarter of 1946; lavatories, 16,500 in the final quarter of 1945 and 18,000 in the first quarter of 1946; soil pipe and fittings, 5,700 tons in the last quarter of 1945 and 6,100 tons in the first quarter of 1946; furnaces, 22,000 in each quarter. Mineral surface shingles show a projected increase of over 10 per cent in the first quarter of 1946 as compared with the final quarter of 1945; insulated siding 16 per cent; panel wall board over 10 per cent; plaster base wall board 12 per cent; gyproc board and lath about 30 per cent., and rock wool over 30 per cent.
The lumber situation is very much improved because of cutbacks in war orders, though dry lumber and millwork may still be relatively scarce temporarily. Brick is one of the really difficult items because of labour shortage, but output is rising.
To illustrate the point that we in Canada are not alone in our troubles about building rfiaterials, I have here some figures on the supply of, and demand for, soil pipe in the United States. They show that, whereas the output of soil pipe has been fairly well maintained during the past twelve months, unfilled orders have more than doubled, increasing from 48 thousand short tons in June of 1944 to 165 thousand short tons in June of 1945.
Housing Act

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
While I am on this subject, I should perhaps say a word or two about the specific complaints that government house building agencies, namely, Wartime Housing Limited and the veterans' land administration, are robbing private builders of supplies. Again I think that there is need for maintaining a proper sense of perspective. As I have said, the objective of a 50,000 house programme in the year following VE-day will probably be attained. How much of this will be built by government agencies cannot be exactly forecast, but the immediate objective of the veterans' land administration is 3,000. houses while about 7,300 houses have been approved under the Wartime Housing programme, most of them since July. In other words, these'government agencies require only a relatively small fraction of the supplies available during the present year, though the impact of their demand has been more or less concentrated in the later part of the building season and this is causing immediate difficulties in some lines.
Occasionally there are allegations that Wartime Housing is stock-piling scarce materials in anticipation of requirements, thus interfering with -the completion of private projects. As my colleague, the Minister of Reconstruction (Mr. Howe) pointed out the other day, whenever such complaints are received they are investigated by officials on the spot. So far no evidence has been found to support them.
Reasons for wartime housing. One thing has been abundantly clear during these past uew months and that is that, for the time oeing at least, private individuals and corporations are willing and anxious to build at least the 50,000 houses for which materials and labour will be available. The limitations on the housing building programme are physical rather than financial. Why, then, it may be asked, has the government considered it necessary to engage in building through Wartime Housing and the veterans' land administration? I do not think I need plead the case for veterans' homes on small holdings under the Veterans' Land Act. This was part of the parliament's rehabilitation programme for veterans and had to be got underway without delay.
As to wartime housing, the considerations were of a different order. The government does not, in general, believe that public housing with dominion ownership represents a sound approach in a country of divided1 jurisdiction in which property and civil rights are the unquestioned field of the provinces under peace-time conditions. Nevertheless, the dom- ,
[Mr. Ilsley.)
inion had, during war time, built some 18,000 houses for war workers, and when certain municipalities requested additional houses for rent to returning veterans and were willing to provide the land without cost and to agree to relatively low payments in lieu of taxes, the government offered to extend its war-time programme, which has been the means of providing decent accommodation at modest rentals for returning servicemen, a need which is urgent and which is not being adequately met otherwise.
This need for rental accommodation for veterans is one of the chief reasons why the government encouraged and made it possible for life insurance companies to get into the rental field immediately. When the National Housing Act amendments are under discussion, I shall explain the technicalities of the various clauses but perhaps it would be useful for me to give a general outline of the problems that arose and that led the government to bring these changes into effect by order in council under the War Measures Act. Hon. members may recall that there are two sections of the act dealing with low rental housing projects. Under section 9, the government is authorized to advance ninety per cent of the lending value of a low rental housing project to a limited dividend housing corporation. The limit on dividends, it wall be recalled, is 5 per, cent. Under section 11, parliament authorized Canadian life insurance companies under dominion jurisdiction to invest up to 5 per cent of their Canadian assets in low or moderate rental housing projects, and guaranteed a net return of 2J per cent per annum on such investments.
Early this summer, when the end of the war with Germany had made it possible to direct more of the country's resources of men and material into housing, conversations were held with officials of the principal life insurance companies in Canada, with a view to ascertaining whether they would be prepared to take advantage of the facilities of the act by embarking at an early date upon a large scale rental housing programme for which there was, and still is, a very great need. The response was favourable though the companies, naturally enough, pointed out that they would prefer to make their major housing investments in the moderate rental field and during periods when building costs were relatively low. It was suggested, however, that in the ordinary course of events it would be desirable if the companies could conduct their operations under section 11 through the medium of subsidiary corporations, and that, if such permission were granted, it would be possible for them to spread the dollars which they were prepared to invest at once over several times

Housing Act
as many houses, by confining themselves for the time being to the low rental field in such a way that their subsidiary corporations would qualify as limited dividend housing corporations thereby becoming eligible for the ninety per cent government advance under section 9.
While a method of operation of this kind had not been anticipated when the act was drafted, it did not appear to do violence to the principles of either section 9 or section 11 of the act. On the one hand, parliament had decided, in order to give a reasonable degree of security to the investment of policyholders' funds, to provide a minimum guarantee of 2| per cent. On the other hand, there seemed to be no reason why a limited dividend corporation owned by a life insurance company should not be eligible for the ninety per cent advance.
Incidentally, one advantage of this type of operation under both sections 9 and 11 of the act is that it will probably result in somewhat lower rentals than if the companies financed the full cost of the project out of their own resources. This follows the fact that a limited dividend corporation is limited to a five per cent dividend on its equity of around ten per cent of the cost, the remainder, financed by the government advance, bearing interest at only three per cent; whereas if the whole of the cost were financed by the companies, the act contemplates that rentals would be fixed at a level sufficient to result in overall earnings of around five per cent.
Moreover, it is well to bear in mind that section 11 limits life insurance company investment in housing projects to five per cent of their assets in Canada, namely an amount of roughly $125 million for all the life insurance companies combined. If the companies were to appropriate a substantial portion of this limited amount during the present period, it would have the effect of circumscribing their operations severely in the years to come and at times when it might be most beneficial to the economy that large scale investments of this kind should be underway. In other words, the forthcoming programme of the life companies may be looked upon as in the nature of an experiment undertaken in a time of emergency which will be of great value in facilitating their own normal operations under section 11 of the act, and will also furnish much needed information in different parts of the country in respect of operations by limited dividend housing corporations under section 9 of the act. I should make it clear that in the contract with these companies there will be a provision that ex-servicemen be given preference as occupants of the projects during the period of shortage.
May I now say a word or two about operations under the National Housing Act. The first point to be noted is that the volume of loans under part I, that is the part of the act dealing with loans for individual house construction, has risen very sharply since the 1944 act came into effect in January of this year, and, although they relate to only a comparatively small fraction of current house building, I think that the act is fulfilling its function in this field and will play an increasingly important role in the months to come. Incidentally, one of the chief purposes of the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation will be to make the advantages of the National Housing Act more widely available throughout the country. On the other hand, apart from the projected emergency operations of the life insurance companies, no loans have been made under those sections of the act relating to low rental projects and no grants have been made for slum clearance. From this the inference might be drawn that these sections of the act have proved to be ineffective and should be recast. I do not want to suggest that the Government would not be prepared at an appropriate time, on the basis of continuing experience, to consider amendments. But it should be borne in mind that one of the chief purposes of these provisions is to stimulate large scale housing operations and that such stimulus is hardly necessary at the present time. As I said earlier, the limitations on house construction at the moment are physical, not financial. The real test of the legislation will come when the present acute congestion begins to disappear, and it becomes feasible to undertake those projects for the improvement of the housing conditions of the lower income groups of the population (involving the replacement of existing buildings), which are so evidently needed.
While this is so, the government is actively interested in the use of all the facilities provided for by the act for increasing the limited supply of modest rental accommodation.
The government's activities in the field of housing have been many-sided and I cannot, in a statement like this, pretend to deal adequately with all phases of it. Control of rentals has been an essential element in the stabilization programme, contributing more probably than any other single control to keeping down the cost of living for tenant families. Some have suggested that we should have gone further and attempted to give the purchaser as well as the tenant of a house protection against rising prices. This was examined most carefully on several occasions, but the conclusion was reached that control on real property values was imprac-
Housing Act

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
tical, though the door has never been definitely closed against some sort of action. I would direct the attention of those hon. members who are interested to the reference book on economic controls prepared for the dominion-provincial conference which contains a section dealing with the problem. I might mention a few of the more obvious difficulties:
1.	Serious discrimination would be involved unless all other forms of capital assets such as the prices of stocks and bonds, were brought under control. House owners would have genuine reason for complaint if house values were controlled while other forms of investment-including for example the prices of farm lands-were not similarly regulated.
2.	It would be extraordinarily difficult to find a suitable yardstick for control. Basic period values are not available generally since only a very small fraction of existing houses is sold in any one year. Local assessments have been investigated but show too much variation as between municipalities to be reliable. Special valuations of each house would take a veritable army of assessors.
The United Kingdom government which, like the United States government, has never attempted to control property values, recently appointed a commission to investigate the problem, and its findings, while not passing judgment on the expediency of introducing controls, confirm our own views as to the difficulty of the task from an administrative standpoint. As I have said, however, it may, in spite of the administrative difficulties, be necessary to institute some form of control.
I should mention, however, that we are now experimenting with a method of getting some control over the prices of some of the new houses by offering to enter into an agreement with builders to take any unsold houses off their hands at a predetermined price, based on estimated costs, if they will undertake to build a substantial group of relatively modest houses approved by the national housing administration, limit their profits on each house and give preference to veterans. This is to be done under the War Measures Act and if it proves to be effective, a suitable amendment to the housing act will be proposed at the next session of parliament.
Closely associated with rental control are the measures taken to protect well-behaved tenants against eviction. These were adopted late in the war and only when it was clear that the situation demanded such a drastic interference with ordinary property rights. It should be possible to restore these rights before long, but under present circumstances we

believe that the action taken was necessary and has helped to stabilize the situation pending relief from the prevailing congestion. I have heard it suggested that both rental and eviction control are hampering house construction, but the fact that all the materials and labour available for building purposes are being used for that purpose indicates that this is not, for the present at least, a significant factor.
To assist municipalities in coping *with their shelter problems by making the most effective use of available unoccupied houses and other suitable buildings, the wartime prices and trade board has had a system of emergency shelter administrators in effect for some time and has recently extended the system to cover the entire country. These administrators have an unenviable and often thankless task, but I have seen enough of their work to know that they are making a real contribution by assisting local bodies in finding accommodation for some of the most urgent cases. As a further contribution the government Is putting buildings which are surplus to war requirements at the disposal of the municipalities and provinces, either at a fraction of their original cost or on a lease basis.
This has been a long statement and I shall say just one word in conclusion. There can be no doubt in anyone's mind, least of all in the minds of those of us who carry the burden of administration, that the shortage of housing is acute and that with the imminent return of further thousands of our men from overseas the situation may well get rvorse before it gets better. This is the situation which we face even though there have been very few periods when so many houses were building as during this first postwar year. But we know that if houses are built at least as quickly as at present-and there is reason to believe that the rate will continue to accelerate for some time-the situation should, after a time, become progressively easier. For its part, the government is determined that it will do all within its powers to assist and to carry into full effect its plans for the better housing of the Canadian people.
Mr. DONALD M. FLEMING (Eglinton): Mr. Speaker, in what I have to say to-day I do not propose to anticipate the provisions of the bill which the Minister of Finance will ask leave of the house to introduce. Of that bill I will say this: We will reserve our judgment upon it, and most of our comment. We will scrutinize it carefully. If it promises improvement in the present unhappy situation,

Housing Act
then, so far as we can we will give it encouragement. To the extent that it does not guarantee some improvement in present conditions, we will criticize it.
We are dealing with a proposal to introduce certain amendments to the National Housing Act. The resolution apparently will also affect other legislation, namely that of 1939 providing for the establishment of a central mortgage discount, bank. In what I have to say to-day I shall try to confine myself largely to the National Housing Act, and, in the light of the statement the minister has just read, to offer some comment upon the form of administration that has been given to that measure.
The National Housing Act is divided into five parts. Part I has to do with encouragement to home ownership. It was designed. to make available substantial loans to those wishing to build houses for their own occupation.
Part II is designed to assist in the creation of rental accommodation, and some terms of that part hold out some hope of assistance in respect of low rental accommodation.
Part III of the act has to do with improvements in rural housing.
Part IV has to do with home improvement and home extension loans.
Part V makes provision for research in the matter of housing and community planning.
The measure was introduced with some fanfare on the part of the government in the session of 1944, and received the royal assent on August 15 of that year, nearly fifteen months ago. It was not proclaimed for five months.
That is the first point, Mr. Speaker. The government waited five months after this statute had received royal assent before it . proclaimed it; and then it did not proclaim the whole act. Part IV of the act has never been brought into effect by proclamation. The concluding section of the statute provides that the various parts shall come into effect by proclamation, and part IV, to which I have referred, has never been brought into operation.
It would be well for us to observe the results of this statute, particularly in the light of the rosy promises that were made and the hopes held out for it by the government at the time of the introduction of the measure. The picture presented to us to-day in the minister's statement might almost be described as a rosy picture. But let- us examine in some detail just what has been accomplished under the administration given
to this measure by the government through the department of the minister who has just delivered the statement. I want to refer particularly to sessional paper 36C tabled in the house on October 10 in reply to certain questions which I had placed upon the order paper. Question 3 was:
What is the total number of houses for which loans have been authorized under part I.
Those were houses to be occupied by owners, and the number given was 3,708. That was the total of the assistance given toward the construction of houses to be occupied by owners from the date this act came into effect until the date of the return. Question 4 was:
How many of such houses have been completed and are now occupied?
The answer was that that information is not in the official government record. In other words, all that has been accomplished, so far as the government's records indicate, is that 3,708 loans have been authorized. There is no information whatever as to the number of houses constructed, or as to the number on which construction has been begun. When we hear rosy statements such as we heard this afternoon, and such as we heard from the Minister of Reconstruction (Mr. Howe) some weeks ago about 50,000 houses being constructed or under construction within the year, it would be interesting to know what small part of that represents houses constructed and what large part represents houses under construction which may not be completed for goodness knows how long, or houses for which loans have been authorized but on which construction has not yet begun. What did this all add up to? Question 5 was:
What is the total amount of the loans authorized under part I?
The answer given was $14,142,185. That was the total amount provided in the entire period during which this statute has been in effect under the present administration in connection with the construction of houses to be occupied by owners.
Let us turn to part II of this act and see just how effective this measure has been in the hands of the present administration in providing for a need that is very sore indeed in the Dominion of Canada, the provision of housing to be occupied by tenants. Question 8 was:
What is the total number of rental housing projects for which loans have been authorized under part II?
The answer was 83 loans for 426 units. A total of 426 housing units for the assistance of people who cannot find homes to rent. That is all the assistance given during the entire period

Of course if they can put before the house figures that indicate the number of loans authorized, perhaps it would be a matter of inference on the part of some that that represented houses constructed. The fact is that the figures do not mean anything of the kind; they simply represent bookkeeping entries in the Department of Finance.
Let us try to reduce the accomplishments under part II to dollars and cents. Question 11 was:
What is the total amount of the loans authorized under part II?
The answer given was $1,567,040. When the measure was introduced in the 1944 session, part II was said to ' be an essential feature designed to give assistance to people who were badly in need of rental housing accommodation. Yet the government has allotted only a million and a half dollars for this purpose. Section 13 of the act provides that the minister may make loans and payments under Part II not exceeding in the aggregate $50,000,000 out of the consolidated revenue fund. The act provided for $50,000,000, but in the time that the measure has been in effect only one and a half millions have been allotted by the government. Does that sound like very energetic application of this act to meet a known need? I leave it to the house to judge.
In his statement this afternoon the minister outlined the government's legislative programme with reference to housing, and we . are to be asked to increase the provisions of section 13 to a total of $125,000,000. As a parliament we are to be asked to increase the amounts that can be provided under that section from $50,000,000 to $125,000,000. Let us measure that in relation to the use the 
government has made of the $50,000,000 it was authorized to use. It has used a million and a half dollars.
Let us look a little further into these answers. Part III had to do with rural housing. Anyone who has made a study of rural housing conditions knows that those conditions are just as much in crying need of redress as are the conditions in our cities and towns, and they are serious in many places. What is the record of the government in its administration of part III of this act.? Question 16 reads:
How many contracts have been entered into by the minister under part III?
The answer given is "one." Only one contract is the record of the administration. I beg your pardon; I am wrong-the answer is "none". I was doing the house, not the minister, an injustice, in making that mistake. Question 17 read:
What is the total number of houses for which loans have been authorized under part III?
The answer given was "one". How a loan was provided for one house under part III and yet no contract was entered into under part III is not clearly indicated, but there is the answer. Then another question:
How many of such houses have been completed?
Again we are told that is not on the government records. Then I asked for the total amount of loans authorized under part III, and the answer given was $5,700.
This is the amazing record of the administration in a field that the minister in his statement this afternoon has admitted to be a field of crying need in the Dominion of Canada.	x
I have indicated what I conceive to be one of the reasons for this dismal failure, and I make no apology for calling it a dismal failure. The reason I have indicated already is that there has been no drive to make the provisions of this act effective to meet a crying need. There has to be a much more sympathetic approach on the part of the administration to the housing problem if anything effective is to be done in this field.

In this respect I point to the plight in which private, builders in Canada to-day find themselves as the result of the measures being applied by the Minister of Reconstruction and his department. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that the way in which the minister has been apply-

Talk about encouragement for building! The private builders in this country have been getting in the main nothing but discouragement from the government by its actions.
I want to refer to an answer given by the Minister of Reconstruction to certain questions I put on the order paper, and which will be found at page 614 of Hansard of October 1. M3r question was this:

The answer was:
Priority assistance is given to Wartime Housing Limited with respect to the purchase of plumbing supplies, roofing, lumber, mill-work, wood shingles, gyproc, rock wool, asphalt _ shingles, cedar grain asbestos shingles, roofing materials, furnaces, nails.
I take it that that was a considered reply, prepared by the officials of the department with due regard for the record.
Now I turn to an answer dealing with the same subject to be found at page 801 of Hansard of October 5. It was a statement made by the Minister of Reconstruction in reply to a question put to him by my leader. The minister said:
There is a great misconception about the matter of priorities. In so far as I am aware, there are no priorities in building materials.
Just to complete this picture of disharmony we have this statement by the minister on page 832 of Hansard of October 9. He is referring to his own remarks which I have just quoted, and says:
In my remarks I stated that there are no building material priorities at all in favour of Wartime Housing Limited. This was not correct.
I should have explained that the government is in fact, giving assistance to Wartime Housing Limited where necessary, and requires producers and distributors in certain cases to deliver to Wartime Housing Limited in priority to other u..ers.
There certainly are priorities in favour of Wartime Housing Limited, and they certainly are being administered in a way which is frustrating builders right along the line. Is it any wonder, that private builders find themselves in such a muddle when the minister himself, in giving the picture to the house of the priorities he administers, gave it in such muddled terms? With the government itself in such a muddle, how can the building industry be in anything but a muddle?
The situation to-day is this, and anyone who has had any contact with building or has made any study of the housing situation in Canada well knows it. Wartime Housing Limited, ipart from priorities, has, as the Minister of Finance said to-day, been a large buyer of material, and let us not underestimate the effect that that has had on the supply of building materials in Canada. What is the effect when Wartime Housing Limited goes to a supplier of building materials and wants to place a big order? Just put yourself in that position, Mr. Speaker. You have certain contacts which have been established over a long period of years with people who depend upon you for their supplies and you want to continue to supply them as they need supplies. Then along comes Wartime Housing Limited, and back of Wartime Housing Limited is always the government. The Minister of Reconstruction is back of Wartime Housing Limited all the time. The result is that these building supply houses to-day are so afraid of ruthless treatment by the administration that they are supplying the demands of Wartime Housing Limited at the expense of private builders all over Canada.

I was speaking about the
causes of this situation, this deplorable situation which we find to-day in the field of housing. I have indicated that the responsibility rests in large measure upon the Department of Finance which is administering the National Housing Act; but it does not rest there alone. I have indicated, I believe, and I think I have given cogent reasons and ample figures to show, that much of the responsibility rests also upon the Minister of Reconstruction. Going back of it all, this situation can be traced to the lack of foresight and lack of courage on the part of the government. Surely they could see that this situation was developing. Why did they not do something about it? This and many of our other problems in this country to-day are traceable to the government's failure to apply a correct and courageous manpower policy in the time of the war. It is small comfort to the people of Canada who badly need housing to-day, who are suffering grave hardship, to be told, "Oh well, after all you are better off than the people in the devastated areas." Well, I should hope we would be. That passage in the statement of the minister this afternoon, I think, will not bring great comfort to our people to-day. It will not bring a great deal of comfort to some of those veterans who, coming back from overseas service, find that they cannot even live with their families. I had a case brought to my notice this week of a man coming back from overseas who could not find accommodation with his family; and this is not an isolated instance.
There are housing conditions of great distress in this country, especially among men from overseas, the men to whom this country owes most. It is on those men that the brunt of this burden is being cast at the present time, traceable to the government's lack of foresight. To-day many of them are buying houses, are devoting their gratuities to the purchase of houses which are really beyond their means, and they are doing it out of sheer desperation. We hold the government largely responsible for the housing crisis in this country.
Moreover we shall welcome an opportunity, and perhaps these proceedings will give us the opportunity at a later stage, of obtaining a great deal more information concerning the situation than has yet been made available to the house.
I have already on three occasions during the present session drawn attention to the provisions of section 30 of the National Housing Act. I am going to read it again:
30. As soon as practicable after the end of each calendar year, the minister shall prepare a report with regard to the administration of this act and the loans made thereunder during the preceding calendar year and the report
Housing Act

shall be laid before parliament forthwith or, if parliament be not then in session, within fifteen days after the commencement of the next ensuing session thereof.
If we are not to have a report for the year 1944, because the government was so tardy in proclaiming the measure, why are we not so told? I asked on September 24 when we were to have the report. The minister said he would look into it; and on September 28, as reported in Hansard, page 540, he said that the report would be brought down at the end of the next week. I referred to it again on October 11; the reference may be found on page 956 of Hansard. But we are still waiting for the report. If there is a report coming, let us have it. Why have we not had it before this? If there is no report coming, why should we not be so told?
I want to offer this suggestion to the Minister of Finance. Since parliament last dealt with the National Housing Act, amendments have been introduced into the act on two occasions by order in council. I refer to order in council P.C. 392, dated January 18, 1945, and P.C. 5794, dated August 30, 1945. I suggest to him that he should give consideration to the status of these amendments. He is proposing certain amendments to the National Housing Act which apparently will completely recast the sections having to do with the administration of the act. It has also been intimated to the house that an amendment will be introduced in connection with the section I referred to earlier, section 13.
Now there is a grave question as to whether the emergency still exists which permits the government to legislate by order in council under the War Measures Act. If the amendments made to the act by order in council depend simply on order in council, then they automatically will come to an end the moment the emergency passes upon which the government's jurisdiction under the War Measures Act depends. If these are good measures, the amendments ought to be introduced in this house, so that parliament may consider them.

I said that so far as the bill is concerned we will resei've our judgment upon it until we receive it and carefully scrutinize its provisions. If the bill does not yet make proper provision for slum clearance measures, I earnestly suggest to the minister that it should not be introduced into the house until proper provision has been made by this measure to undertake in an adequate and concerted way the clearance of slums in Canada. The present National Housing Act does not make provision for the clearance of slums. You will never clear slums under that act as it stands, and if w7e are going to undertake the revision of the act I say that we must make sure that the great omission from the act of 1945 is remedied and cured now.
As I said earlier, I do not want to anticipate the provisions of the bill, but if it should result that the administration of housing is confided to a corporation presided over by a board of directors, I hope the minister will see to it that women and veterans are represented on the board. I am naive enough to say to the house that I do not believe you will ever have an adequately sympathetic or energetic application of the provisions of the housing legislation to meet the needs of the country unless you have women participating in the administration of the measure.

There is no man in Canada who has all the information on housing, and women are very close to this problem. I repeat therefore that you will never have a properly balanced administration, if you are going to appoint a board of directors, unless you have women represented on that board. I offer that suggestion to the minister, and I hope that veterans also will be represented on any board that is set up-veterans, those on whom, most unfairly, the burden of housing conditions is being cast to-day.
When we approach this bill we shall want to be shown how housing and the business of a mortgage discount bank or corporation can be combined. We do not want to see any more confusion introduced into the administration of the national housing policy. Goodness knows there is enough confusion there now; let us not create any more. Again, and on this I take it I am on common ground with one observation at least that fell from the lips of the Minister of Finance this afternoon, we want to see the housing administration so set up that it will not be farther removed from the control of parliament, farther removed from the place where parliament will have its opportunity to discharge its

Housing Act
duty to the people of Canada and to review the policy being applied by the national housing administration.
Parliament has a great responsibility in this matter, but I am not speaking only of parliament's responsibility in the matter of supervision of expenditures, because in my humble opinion that is not the most important consideration in respect of housing. There is a consideration far more important, and that is the provision of legislation to meet the social need, the need for decent housing accommodation for people who in many cases are unable to provide that accommodation for themselves. We have also a responsibility as parliament to see to it that everything is done that can be done to assist these people.
And now, Mr. Speaker, I have finished, but for a word in conclusion. If the bill the minister introduces offers any hope of emancipation of the country from the muddle into which the housing policy has been allowed by the government to fall, we will welcome it as far as it goes. If it does not hold out any such promise, we shall have to discharge our duty and give it close and critical scrutiny.

subtopic: CENTRAL MORTGAGE AND HOUSING CORPORATION- DISCOUNTING FACILITIES
speechtext:
I find myself in agreement with much that has been said by the member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming). His analysis of the shortcomings of the National Housing Act as it has operated to date has been carefully presented. I think he has performed a valuable service in placing on the order paper certain questions that have been answered. I was disappointed, however, that he did not have some more constructive suggestions to offer in connection with Canada's very critical housing problem at the present time. Within the memory of most of us we had in Canada at one time a Conservative government. It was not then Progressive Conservative, but there was a Conservative government when there were no war-time controls, when we did not have a shortage of lumber or of building materials, when there was no shortage of labour; and yet the Conservative administration seemed to be even more completely paralyzed than the present government.
During the years from 1930 to 1935, when we had the Conservative government in office in Canada, when there was a world-wide depression, the governments in the United Kingdom, the United States, Sweden, France and Holland realized that there was an opportunity then to clear out some of the disgraceful slums that have been a blot on society. In the United Kingdom for example, taking 1929 as the base, they increased the construction of houses from 100 in that year
to 114 in the worst year of the depression, while in Canada we dropped from 100 to 70 in 1930, to 47 in 1931, to 16 in 1932, and we reached an all-time low in 1933 of 9-7.
We had a slum problem in 1933 that was practically identical with the slum problem that now exists, and, as I said, we did not have any controls to worry about. If the private builders were able to do the job, there was no reason why they did not do it during the thirties. I agree with the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) that if we could remove those controls, the private builders would really go to work. I have no doubt that we would be building some $25,000 to $35,000 houses immediately, but we have only a limited amount of building material available and if this material is to be available in all parts of Canada as fairly as possible someone has to take the responsibility of seeing that no one will be building a $25,000 house until something is done for people in the lower brackets.
I am not offering any defence for the administration; I am trying to get across the point that the removal of our controls would add to the problems rather than solve them. We would enable the real estate dealers and contractors to have a field day. They would be able to make up for the war years, although some of them did fairly well even during the war years.
Let me remind the house that there was nothing to stop the private builders from entering this field in 1940, 1941 and 1942. The shortage of materials was not very critical at that time; and believe me, this administration we now have did not set up Wartime Housing for the fun of it. They have friends in the building trades too. The only reason we have Wartime Housing Limited in Canada is that the contractors, the private builders, just were not prepared to build houses in Windsor, Hamilton, Halifax and Vancouver, in the centres in Canada where we had a serious shortage. I think it is unfair to suggest [DOT] that if they now had the green light they would step into the breach and solve our problem.
If we divide the population of this country, or of any country, into three groups, the people in the upper third of our income bracket will be able to finance and build their houses without assistance from the government in any shape or form. Until we have a change in the supply situation it is important that rigid controls be maintained to see to it that those in the upper third of the bracket do not have four or five rooms per person in the home while in Ottawa returned veterans have to live eight to nine persons in a one or
Housing Act

two-roomed house. Therefore I think the speech delivered by the hon. member for Eglinton has focused attention on an obvious weakness in the government's housing programme, but it did not offer any solution.
Members of this group always welcome any legislation that will face up to the problem. It is unfortunate that, although the National Housing Act was assented to on August 15, 1944, people in Canada have not been able to see that this legislation has made any material difference to our situation.
I might draw'the attention of hon. members to an interesting article in the last issue of Maclean's magazine which was written by Blair Fraser under the title of " Hovels for Heroes." I believe this article says everything that needs to be said about Canada's housing problem. I have tried to get across these ideas all during the war period, emphasizing, in addition to participating on the battlefield and supplying materials, the necessity of providing adequate houses for those working in war industries and in the areas that have become congested as a result of shifts in our population.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) indicated there were other more pressing responsibilities. In my opinion the government of the day failed to attach sufficient importance to the providing of adequate housing as a part of our war contribution. He mentioned that every country of the world has a situation similar to the one we have in Canada; but I venture to say that in most countries they have past experience that will enable them to deal with the problem much more quickly than Canada.
The Minister of Finance mentioned certain constitutional problems that exist in Canada; that the provinces would no doubt object to the federal government carrying on activities such as Wartime Housing as a part of our permanent policy. I have repeatedly suggested that the federal government should take the initiative in convening a conference of representatives from the provinces and municipalities to face up to this problem.
As I said before, I think those in the upper third of the income brackets would be able to get all the materials and labour that would be their fair share. Legislation such as is provided by the National Housing Act would be very useful in seeing that the lending institutions are kept happy, serving the third of our population in the middle group. Private builders have a chance to cater to these sections of our economy, but fully a third of the Canadian people cannot look forward to
rMr. Nicholson.]
having modern low-cost housing under any legislation that now exists or that is being proposed.
The last time I discussed the question in the house I suggested that the federal government should take the initiative in setting up five experimental units in Canada. I feel sure that the provinces and municipalities concerned would give full cooperation to this kind of experiment, so that in Toronto and Montreal, for example, a model section of the city might be planned and five hundred low cost houses built and made available to people in the lowest income brackets in the community. It would require a subsidy. I believe that the provinces, the municipalities and the federal government should all participate in seeing that the housing was made available, so that returning veterans and lower paid workers could look forward to having modern, comfortable housing at rents that they could afford to pay.
I suggested that in Winnipeg, Vancouver and Halifax from two to three hundred permanent houses might be built as a part of an overall experimental plan. The federal government would be justified in appropriating sufficient funds to undertake to do this job under a set-up similar to that of Wartime Housing.
I have been critical of a good deal of the work done by Wartime Housing, but I never for one moment suggested that it would be a good thing if we -had not had Wartime Housing, and I cannot share the opinions expressed by some of the Progressive Conservatives this afternoon that the administration should wash its hands of Wartime Housing and not take responsibility for the eighteen or nineteen thousand families in Canada who are living in those houses. I know that some of the private builders in the country insisted that those houses should be torn down six months after the cessation of hostilities. It would probably provide a better market for those interested in real estate and in the building trade to have those eighteen thousand houses tom down, but I submit it would not be a popular move in Canada with winter coming on.
