speechtext:
That has been my
opinion, that they will become potential slums. But in the meantime they are more comfortable than houses available at similar rents, or in many instances double the rents, in the centres in which they are now located.
I suggest that some organization such as Wartime Housing might be given authority to construct some experimental units, so that on

Housing Act
our own soil in Canada we might have a demonstration of what town planning, mass production and a plan would mean. If that were done we would have some basis of deciding whether or not the claim that C.C.F. members have made in the past is true, namely, that private builders will never in Canada do anything effective to clear out slum areas and to make living quarters available for people who live in those slum districts.
I also wish to mention the failure to deal with the problem in rural Canada. During the summer a family in my constituency had the misfortune to lose their house and the contents thereof by fire. Their only son was soon expected back from overseas, and they wondered if it would not be possible to obtain a loan under the new legislation which had been passed. I got in touch with Ottawa and outlined the details. It was suggested that if these people would get in touch with the local bank it should be possible to obtain the necessary loan. They carried out those instructions, but they found that the local bank was not interested in making a loan.
My information is that the people who can get assistance under the legislation for rural housing are those who do not need it. They could go to a bank on their own account and borrow money, or they might have sufficient resources without securing a loan.
When the bill is before the house I suggest that the minister should be prepared to give us a great deal more detail as to what machinery he has in mind to make it possible to tackle rural housing in a progressive fashion. He should give details, too, as to what we can expect from ihe lending institutions.
The hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) might have gone a good deal farther than he did in criticizing the government for going to the private lending institutions, and giving them out of the federal treasury ninety per cent of the - capital to be invested in housing. To me that appears to be an abdication of responsible government. It is an admission that we are bankrupt of ideas, that we cannot face up to this problem ourselves, and that we have to turn it over to the insurance companies of Canada so that they may set up subsidiary corporations to look after our business.
Since the government's policy seems to t>e fairly well decided upon, I suggest that the minister should be expected to give some indication as to what provisions will be made for the building of houses in congested centres on the prairies or in smaller communities anj'-where. I have no doubt that in the large centres I have mentioned loans will be made
available, I fear, however, that under the present legislation, as in the past, people in rural communities and small towns and villages will find it difficult to benefit from the act. The minister should give us some details in that respect.
I hope, too, that he will give particulars regarding the over-all plan for the next year. He has mentioned that the aim is to have 50,000 houses constructed during the first twelve months after the cessation of hostilities. It is not too soon to expect him to tell us how many will be built in the second twelve months. I hope when we have the bill before us, the minister will give us information on these points.
In conclusion, may I express my regret that the government has not seen fit to provide legislation to ensure that definite action is taken in clearing slums and providing adequate shelter for those large numbers of Canadian people in the lower income brackets, who have not a chance in the world of looking forward to being able either to rent, or to build a house, or to buy one, with building costs as they are at the present time.

maintopic: NATIONAL HOUSING ACT
subtopic: CENTRAL MORTGAGE AND HOUSING CORPORATION- DISCOUNTING FACILITIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had not expected that the debate on the resolution would have been prolonged to this extent. I had thought that such debate would take place on the motion for second reading. However, since the matter is now being discussed in full I shall take a few minutes to express my views.
We have listened to two speeches and, like the hon. member who has just taken his seat, I should like to congratulate the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) upon his presentation. Although the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Nicholson) criticized the hon. member for Eglinton for not having offered any constructive ideas, I must say I looked in vain for any such suggestions in his own speech. So far I have been unable to discover any.
The government has sponsored three types of building, namely national housing, wartime housing and veterans housing, and I should like to say only a brief word in respect of each type. As most hon. members know I come from the west, near the city of- Calgary, in which a good deal of this type of building is taking place, and I have watched with interest what has been done. On several occasions I' have looked into the building of these houses, and I want to say about national housing-and I speak only from the point of view of construction-that I believe the houses built under that programme are far superior to those built under either of the remaining
Housing Act

two types. It is true, though, that even under the national plan improvements could be made.
There are many criticisms in connection with national housing concerning points which I believe to be of only minor importance. For instance, before coming to this session I visited a house being built under the national housing plan, and found that the contractor in charge was criticizing the government severely for stipulating ten-inch cement walls in the construction. He thought that such construction increased the price unnecessarily. I pointed out to him that while to a degree I could agree with him that ten-inch walls in the construction of residences, and especially in western Canada, were unnecessary, the fault, if it could be so described, was a good one.
The material being used in the construction of national houses is the best that is being used in any of the government housing projects. When I say it is the best, I mean that it is only a cheap, second-grade material. I am referring to the dimension lumber. Of course that is true not only of houses built under the national scheme, but of every type of house being built in Canada, of which I have visited a great number. Surely this is a shame.
The hon. member for Eglinton referred to the exporting of Canadian building materials. I am told by reliable lumbermen in both Calgary and Edmonton-and I take it that the same condition applies throughout Canada -that the best of our number one building material is being shipped out, and that we are being given second and third grades. Yet the people of this country are paying first-grade prices.
I have seen materials sent back to lumber yards-and I am not blaming the yards-[DOT] which should not have been put even in the construction of a garage, but which were supposed to be used in the construction of national, wartime, and veterans houses. There is nothing they can do about it. The lumber yards simply say, "You will take this material or nothing," or in a great many cases they say, "Send it back." Generally speaking, the people who are building these houses are having to pay big prices. Houses being built under national housing now cost around $6,000, when in my opinion they should cost from $4,500 up to not more than $5,000. Some of these men are veterans and they are building under the national housing plan, but particularly is this true of veterans' houses and, more so, wartime houses. In my estimation they are getting a pretty raw deal

because they are being charged much more for these houses than they are actually worth.
I think the government should be informed about one thing in case they do not know it already. In many instances the owners, in the case of national housing, and the prospective owners, in the case of veterans' houses, are not satisfied with the plans and specifications. After a house is started a man may go to the contractor and say that he does not want a certain plan, that he wants a room changed, that the kitchen is too small and he wants it in another position. What happens? Quite often the contractor will agree to make certain improvements in the house. I do not know how he gets around the inspector because he is certainly getting away from the plans and specifications; I know it is being done because I have been in the houses and seen it.
The result is that because of these extras the owner must pay the contractor about $1,000 more than the contract calls for. When the lending company comes along to put a mortgage on the house it does not mind because the house is much more improved; it is a finer house than the original contract called for, and their protection is that much greater. But it puts the owner of the house in an untenable position and I think the government should put more protection into effect.
As I indicated, the materia! going into national houses is, in most instances, very good. I think in all instances where I have seen national houses being built they were being built by private contractors. In those particular instances the workmanship was good and the material was just as good as that going into private houses being built, possibly just across the street. I think they will be worthwhile projects. But in the case of veterans' houses the material is not so good, nor is the plan of construction.
The hon. member who just resumed his seat was, I think, a little in favour, if not wholeheartedly in favour of mass production. I do not know whether he has watched this closely or not, but in the case of veterans houses which are being built under a mass production plan the workmanship is very much inferior. In the case of national housing, the material is good in most cases. Fir is used where they can get it, but in the case of wartime housing, spruce is used exclusively. Anyone who has had any experience in housing knows that it is almost impossible to keep spruce from shrinking. In ninety-nine per cent of the cases the spruce used is exceedingly wet and green, and in some cases they have almost forgotten to cut off the leaves.

Housing Act
Full basements are being put under these new veterans houses, and that is a good thing. However, as far as the dimension stuff that is being used is concerned, I think the returned men who are putting their last cent into homes -mind you, these homes are running from $4,000 to $6,000-will get an awful stinging. These houses will be cold and they will start pulling away. They are bound to do that when the green lumber begins to shrink. Just ordinary nails were used instead of coated nails which would have assisted a little bit when such green lumber was being used. I think these are some of the things that should be looked into.
As far as wartime housing is concerned, the material Being used is much on a par with that used for veterans houses; it is exclusively spruce. Along with' the shrinking and twisting of the material this is certainly not going to be conducive to good homes.
Another thing that should be mentioned with regard to the general construction of these houses is the continued use of footings rather than complete basements in connection with wartime housing units. Especially in the west, I do not think any house should be built unless it has a full basement. If a veteran buys a home under Wartime Housing it will be only a matter of time before he will want a full basement. It will be an exceedingly difficult and costly proposition to put a full basement under the house once it is erected. It can be done, but it means unnecessary expense. The construction of proper basements would prove a great asset to wartime houses. [DOT]
Some of these house are being built on posts. Surely the government knows from experience what happens when a house is built on posts. We only have to go to Hull to get an example of what has happened to some of these wartime houses. I visited some of the houses in Hull, and I found that in less than a year after they were constructed it was impossible to close the outside doors because one corner of the house had sunken away, the floor had buckled or something else had happened. Why we should go ahead and continue to build houses on footings, even though they may be of cement blocks of eighteen to twenty-four inches in thickness, is more than I can say.
I do not want to detain the house too long, but I should like to speak for a minute about the difficulties some builders are having in obtaining building material. The first speaker this afternoon referred to priorities. I think he covered that subject fairly thoroughly and I shall not go into it any farther. I agree with what he said in that regard. Wartime Housing has the priority. I think it is perfectly all right to give priorities to returned men; I am not criticizing that at all, but under the priorities scheme for wartime and veterans' houses the government has made it possible for large quantities of scarce building materials to be piled up and allowed to stay for months on end without being used. I have actually seen this because I have kept close watch.
I have seen building materials set aside for veterans' houses, materials such as lath, shingles, plumbing fixtures, and other things of that type, piled up on the premises with just a few boards over them and allowed to stay for months at a time without being used, when right across the street would be a private dwelling, with the roof on and completely enclosed1, already stuccoed if it is to be a stucco house. These buildings are just sitting there waiting because they cannot get the materials that are piled up just across the road. In a case of that kind, when the house is ready for plumbing or lathing or shingling, the materials required that are there in existing stores should be made available so that construction can proceed. If there are two houses equally near to being finished- they both need gyproc lath, we will say-the veteran undoubtedly should be given priority. There are cases like that right now in the city of Calgary. I think I am conservative- and I do not mean Progressive Conservative-

speechtext: You are improving.

maintopic: NATIONAL HOUSING ACT

speechtext:
Improving in my teachings perhaps because I think we have been able to teach the Progressive Conservatives some things. I was going on to say that there are at least a hundred houses in Calgary waiting to be finished and unable to get the necessary materials. They could be occupied within two months if they had the lath and the plumbing. They have the roof on; all the outside work is finished, but they lack these other materials. The government may say that these materials are in short supply, but I say that this stuff in short supply has sat there on the hill for two or three months.
As I said, if there are two houses that are ready for lathing, and one is a veteran's house and the other a civilian's, I would not hesitate a second to give the veteran priority. But why hold up all these other houses until the veteran's house reaches the stage where it needs the materials which the civilian house could use at once?
I have already brought to the attention of the minister of supply this question of shortage of materials when the materials are actually in storage. I am told on good authority, by a reliable businessman who has a large interest in this kind of work, that he has
Housing Act

seen three carloads of gyproc lath stored in Calgary for Wartime Housing. It is sometimes hard to find out just who owns this material or whether it is stored to be used later in veterans houses. At any rate, this particular material has been stored there for a long time, and without breaking any confidence I can say that the minister of supply received a long-distance phone call about it and promised to investigate immediately, *which he did. He sent a man out there, and so far as I can learn the man made a proper report. Unfortunately, however, when he came to investigate where the material was located, the material was no longer there but had been moved somewhere else, and the minister, I understand, is now investigating that. I do not blame the minister particularly for that, because I can see how it might happen. He is being given the run-around. That is with regard to gyproc lath.
Take plumbing. The same is true there. A plumber told me that he had shipped several wash-basins which are in short supply, to the Currie Supply depot in Calgary or the place up there on the hill. It stood there for some considerable time, and he told me that up to the time he was speaking to me they had not been used. But he was compelled to supply them.
I am told that between four and five hundred bath-tubs are stored in Calgary. Whether that is true or not I do not know. I have asked the minister to get the information for me. The man who told me that is a reliable businessman, one of the largest in the city of Calgary. I wanted to know the facts in that case, and so I went to the only proper place, to the minister.
Here is another thing which may assist the minister in getting some of these houses finished. About two weeks ago I was talking to a plumber who had great difficulty in getting bath-tubs. He went for a trip to the United States, and when he came back he told me there was no shortage of bath-tubs in the United States, that you could walk into any store and buy one. That is just what he did. He went into a big store in Seattle and asked about bath-tubs. They said, "Yes; -we have lots of them." Accordingly he bought a bath-tub and shipped it to one of his customers in Calgary. Under the regulations he could get only one. so that he got someone else to get another one for him. But that is not a good way of doing business. The government might well look into this matter and make it possible to have plumbing equipment that is available in the United
[Mr. Johnston. J
States shipped to Canada where it is in short supply. That should apply to any type of plumbing equipment which is in short supply in Canada and in long supply in the United States.
The hon. member who preceded me this afternoon spoke of private builders not doing a very good job in trying to clear away slum areas. But that has not been my experience.
I 'think the finest type of house being built to-day is being built by private contractors for private individuals. When a contractor gets a contract to build fifty or sixty houses he is producing on a mass production scale.
I do not think that is a good plan when it comes to building private houses. The minister has had some experience in this matter and knows that you cannot build the side of a house out of ordinary spruce lumber, spruce ship-lath, spruce siding, using ordinary two and a half inch nails. Yet they are building that side down on the floor; then they put the windows in, set it up on the rough floor, then build the other part, set it up on the rough floor, and then nail the two together. That is not good construction. I do not think it will stand up. I have watched very carefully this type of houses under construction. Not only do I think it is a poor type of construction, but I think the wrong principle is involved in distributing contracts for the mass production of private homes. I have heard many complaints, especially in the city of Calgary, where I live, by competent contractors who have proved their worth in the field and who cannot get a share of this contract work. They say: "Why should such-and-such a contractor" -I am not going to name him because the * minister will know some of those to whom I am referring-"get a contract to build fifty or sixty houses and we cannot get any?" I suppose it is'because he goes in for mass production, but there are other contractors who want a share in this work but who for some reason or another do not get any of these contracts.
Of course, when a man goes in for mass production and builds fifty or sixty houses, he gets a priority on labour and on building materials, and he can go ahead and pile up his building materials so that the progress of his work will not be hindered. But the private contractor across the street cannot get anything, even though he sees that material piled [DOT] upon the hill and not being used, and it may not be used for five or six weeks or two or three or even six months. That is discourag-

Housing Act
mg to private builders. Some of the things I have heard them say about the government's plan of building in that way I would not want to repeat here, because they would be unparliamentary. But I think the private builder has a logical complaint, and it is something which should be looked into.
The remarks I have made are the result of actual experience I have had in visiting these buildings. As I have said, I think the national houses are good houses considering the type of material-which is only second-grade lumber-that they have to put into them, and which should not be in houses costing around six or seven thousand dollars apiece. That is a lot of money to invest in a private home, and the materials should be good. But the workmanship is satisfactory. As regards the wartime housing and that allocated to veterans, I do not think the lumber used is of a type which should be used at all. The boys are getting an awful stinging. I do not understand why, if we are to build these houses and the fellows are spending their hard-earned money to buy them, we do not put in good material, because these are the homes in which these men are going to live and raise their families.
Not only that, but if you build these houses of cheap construction-they are not financially cheap-in some of these city areas you will create the very thing which the last speaker attributed to the operations of some private contractors; that is, you will have slum areas, for in no time at all these houses will go to rack and ruin, and five to ten years from now they will look like old shacks. That statement is not true of the national houses. The [DOT]ones 1 have seen are a good type, and while they are costing more than I think they should, they are much better built than either the veterans houses or the wartime housing.
I am not going to detain the house any longer, but I shall have a few things to say when the bill comes up.

maintopic: NATIONAL HOUSING ACT
subtopic: CENTRAL MORTGAGE AND HOUSING CORPORATION- DISCOUNTING FACILITIES
speechtext:
I wish to refer briefly to the position of the municipalities, urban, suburban and rural, on housing. Away back in 1935, as the result of my resolution, a committee of the House of Commons was appointed to consider .the whole question of housing and reconstruction to aid building. It held quite a number of meetings and heard some of the most prominent of officers-Mr. D'Arcy Leonard among others-of the principal loan and mortgage companies and, indeed, experts from all over the world, and made its report to the high court of parliament.
Housing is probably the most important problem which any country has to deal with.
The way in which it has been handled in this country amounts to a public scandal. So far as the housing situation is concerned, I do not believe in the present cumbersome policy of the government; it has been weighed in the balance and found wanting. Take, for example, ward1 9, Toronto, the district in which I live; it has been a paradise for the loan companies and the mortgage companies with the highest interest rates. The people who live there have been charged as much as 6i and 7 per cent for loans, and they are sick and tired of loan and mortgage companies.
The city of Toronto has pioneered in the matter of housing reform. No agency relates more to public health than proper housing. We have had splendid health officers in Doctor Hastings and those who have succeeded him.
What was done? From 1937 to this war $82 million was spent on housing by the government through the banks. I opposed in this house the government of Canada going into vast expenditures for the creation of a large public housing body centred here in Ottawa, with clerks and stenographers and officers all over the country. I contended that the work could be done far better, first, by aiding the municipalities, and second, by lending the money, through a government guarantee, to the banks at a low rate of interest, not to exceed three per cent.
As I mentioned, some $82 million was spent on that policy, and there was a big building wave all over our city and suburbs. One reason it was a success in Toronto was that the city provided by transportation, water, sewers, health laws and suburban good roads, the key to modern housing schemes. The city also started its own civic street cars and bought out the radials, started the buses and gave at cost and a single fare all Toronto by a civic system, whereas before that there were six or seven different fares in greater Toronto, now the present city, and it carried out a good road programme for fifteen miles outside. And let me say that housing in any community, be it urban, suburban or rural, cannot be separated from the problem of roads and transportation generally, of light, water, schools, sanitation, police and fire protection. The city of Toronto went to work north, east, south and west and cleaned out a lot of light and power and all transportation franchises, not only in the city but in the counties of Ontario, York and Peel, and linked those places up in a' civic system of transportation with radials and buses.
Housing Act

a new front. If, as the Canadian Corps say, they had the labour and materials, it would help them materially.
If the government would give the municipalities some help along the lines I have indicated, it would be far better, because Toronto has had to do all this work alone. Transportation is the key to the housing problem because without it houses cannot be built, and there must also be proper services available.
The other day I had a return with regard to a soldier about -whom I had asked some questions. He wanted to go into a retail shop, but there were no such shops that he could rent. I asked, what aid is the government giving to ex-servicemen to go back to their retail stores, and would it not be far better if they did? No aid is given. The soldiers received a long letter from the wartime prices and trade board telling them what to do. If that is all they can do they might as well not have answered. It was just a scrap of paper. No soldier can get a retail store with that; for want of a housing policy nobody can help them.
The government ought to do something about housing. They ought to remove the irksome controls on property holders. I represent a district where sixty-seven per cent of the people in- the district used to own their own homes. Pretty nearly two-thirds of the population of the city owned their own homes. The control system and irksome controls have ruined real estate. If the government wants to do something they should remove some of the irksome controls which have been fastened on the real estate -owners, large and small, of the larger cities.
I believe that this resolution is too late. It will not facilitate the building of houses. It will lead to a large amount of money being spent on organization and head office staff. It mentions the sum of $25,000,000. I do not believe it will aid one iota in solving the housing situation in any municipality. If the gov-erment would do something to control and regulate further the loan and mortgage companies, get cheap money, put some body over them to control them, they would do far more for housing than the proposed resolution does.
I regret very much having to offer these criticisms to the proposed resolution. But having had an extensive experience in the housing situation and in supplying municipal services in a large city, I feel I must give voice to my beliefs. The city from which I come was the pioneer city in housing and social work; it has branched out; it has given sewers, water and health services, police protection, fire protection and other things to the suburban municipalities. It is doing the
[Mr. Church.1
same to-day with buses, radials, roads and all these things. I believe that the government should go to the support of the larger municipalities like Toronto with direct federal aid for these works along the lines I have indicated. In that way we will do more to get houses built than by any other agency.
In conclusion, I wish to say that I noticed two years ago Mr. Churchill had a proposal to build in Great Britain five hundred thousand pre-fabricated houses. As a result of our not being ready with labour and materials, industries in Canada received very few of those orders from the old country; the United States got pretty nearly the whole.
The housing situation is the key to good health for men, women and children. Without a sanitary house there can be no other freedom or liberty for the toilers and workers of this country. I do hope that something will be done to aid the larger municipalities that I have mentioned to accomplish some relief in the coming winter, because it is going to be a very severe one. If we get a cold winter like last winter I do not know what we shall da. The government no doubt will have to provide some form of direct relief and give some direct aid to the larger municipalities aj a relief measure to tide them over the coming winter.

subtopic: CENTRAL MORTGAGE AND HOUSING CORPORATION- DISCOUNTING FACILITIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I shall endeavour to address my remarks, which I shall try to keep brief, to the specific resolution now before the house.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) is proposing to introduce a bill to provide for the setting up of a central mortgage and housing corporation together with $25 million for the paid-up capital of this corporation. In his remarks this afternoon when presenting the resolution to the house the minister said that the government had now reached the stage where it was going into the housing business, and that that was the reason for having made the decision to set up a corporation which, in part, would take over the functions of the Minister of Finance, as set out under the National Housing Act.
It is only partly true, it seems to me, to say that the government is going into the business of housing, so far as this piece of legislation or, indeed, the National Housing Act itself is concerned. What the government is doing is to go into the business of seeking

Housing Act
to finance the building of homes. To the extent that the government at least feels that it is going into the business of housing, I offer my commendation. I feel that it is being pressed by events to realize that there is a responsibility on the part of government in connection with this important phase of the life of our people.
I shall not take time to add further to what my desk-mate, the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Nicholson) had to say in reply to the remarks of the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming), except that I wish to add that surely this is no time for our turning the clock backwards. We have had plenty of experience with the failure of private enterprise to provide homes for our people. On the other hand we have seen, under the necessities of war, that when there are things that are absolutely needed for the country as a whole, the responsibility to get those things done rests upon the government.
The government during war years did face up to the responsibility of seeing to it that the needs of the war were met. We in this group consider-and in that, of course, we'are not alone, so far as our feeling is concerned; it is in the matter of getting these things done that we differ-that the provision of homes for the Canadian people is just as imperative a peacetime need as were munitions and supplies imperative war-time needs. So, to the extent that the government is moving in the direction of setting up the machinery for going into the business of housing, I cannot but. welcome this measure.
I suppose hon. members will feel I atn simply saying the same old thing when I add that to me it does not go far enough. But that is exactly the case, and it is the principal criticism I would offer about this measure. This afternoon in his speech the minister gave some of the details as to how this new corporation might function. First of all, he pointed out that it would take his place as Minister of Finance, in the operations listed under the National Housing Act; and then he said that it would perform a discounting function for loan and mortgage companies.
He referred to discussions or conferences that had been held with the life insurance companies as to why they had not taken fuller advantage of the National Housing Act for the building of homes. If I understood him correctly, out of those conferences came the proposal that the life insurance companies might set up subsidiary corporations which, in effect, would be limited dividend housing corporations, and that in turn this central 47696-95
mortgage and housing corporation could assist those life insurance subsidiary companies in the business of housing.
It is at that point the government has not yet been sufficiently impressed by the events of our time. Rather than having the central mortgage and housing corporation, which is to be a crown company, deal with other new bodies to be set up by private life insurance companies, it seems to me that the functions of the corporation the minister now proposes to set up should be enlarged to those of a public housing authority.
I believe I must make with regard to this proposal the same criticism of its shortcomings that I made in August, 1944, when the National Housing Act was presented to parliament. I complained at that time that the measure then under consideration was more in the nature of an act to assist the mortgage companies and the life insurance companies than it was to provide for the building of homes. On that occasion I went on to express my fear that the act would not result in the thing we really want, namely the building of homes for the Canadian people.
I feel quite frankly that the action of the minister now in bringing in these proposals, and also in his proposed amendment to the National Housing Act, is an admission that, to put it mildly, there were shortcomings in his earlier legislation, and that it has not done all he had hoped it would do. In other words, it has failed to do the job.
I thought when he was describing this afternoon the discussions with the life insurance companies that in a mild way he was telling of what amounted to a strike on their part, a refusal or the contention that under the terms of the act they could not do the thing the government wanted, namely, facilitate the building of homes in this country. Recognizing the shortcomings of the act passed in 1944, the minister makes the further proposal for setting up this central mortgage and housing corporation. Having been right in my former criticism, I offer it again. I fear that the minister is still fighting shy of the real solution of this problem when he refuses to set up a central public housing authority with funds and power definitely to go into the building of homes for our Canadian people. Nonetheless, I certainly want to support this measure, partly on the theory that half a loaf is better than none and partly because I believe that this is the beginning of the setting up of the kind of governmental machinery that can be used in the name of the people as a whole to do something that (he government should do for the people of Canada.

Housing Act

In connection with this whole question of housing it seems to me that we have become bogged down in technical details; we have been too much hampered by a concern to use the existing machinery, the mortgage companies, the insurance companies and so on rather than allowing ourselves a little play of imagination as to what we should be doing in the field of housing. To me the providing of really good homes in the best locations with all the community facilities that can be provided in terms of modern community planning should be the major concern of this government in the matter of housing. It is not good enough to talk about a few slum clearance projects here and there, or the building of temporary accommodation. I repeat what I said in an earlier speech in this present session; we should have the imagination to take an area such as I could indicate in my own constituency, clean out the kind of homes that are there and build in their places a modern, model community with the best homes, and the best of educational, recreational and health facilities for those who do the country's work and deserve for themselves and their families the best of living conditions.
It takes imagination to do that sort of thing, but it has been attempted with a considerable measure of success by some of the public housing authorities in the United States. It has been attempted also on quite a large scale in the United Kingdom. It could and should be done here; in fact it should be one of our major post-war concerns. We are all interested in maintaining full employment ' in the years that lie ahead, and I suggest (hat this is the place to use a little imagination and launch, not just the building of a few thousand homes, but the creation of housing projects all over this country so that our Canadian people can be placed in the best kind of homes, in the best kinds of communities that modern architects and engineers can design.
That will never be done with the appropria-ating of such a small sum as $25,000,000. It will never be done by setting up only an intermediary crown corporation and expecting private enterprise, which has so failed our people in the past, to- do it. It will be done only by using the same kind of imagination that this government used-I say this without hesitation-in setting out to meet the needs of the war.
I was a little surprised this afternoon when the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) quoted from a letter dated August 20, 1945, addressed to the government by the Trades and

Labour Congress of Canada. If I heard him correctly, his inference was that the quotation was in support of giving private enterprise a free hand in the matter of housing. I should like to quote again the item he read; it is the fourth item in a series of proposals which were made by the Trades and Labour Congress of Canada to the government. It reads:
That restrictions be lifted from building materials and that the construction of homes be carried on with the same effort, ingenuity and dispatch as was displayed in the production of urgently needed war materials.
That might be said to be entirely neutral on the question as to whether housing is to be undertaken by public or private enterprise. However, I would point out two things. First, this is an appeal to the government for action; there is no reference to private enterprise at all. Second, it reminds the government that when war came and there were things that were urgently needed, the government used effort, ingenuity and dispatch. Now that peace is here and we all recognize the tremendous need for rehousing the people of Canada .in the finest and most modern communities we can build, I should like to see used the same effort, ingenuity and dispatch. I should like to see the employment of the imagination and capacities that our architects, engineers, scientists and technicians have.
Whether or not the government will accept immediately my suggestion that the powers, of this corporation be enlarged to those of a public housing authority, I dare to hope that the step we are taking to-night by way of setting up this corporation foreshadows better things to come. I say once again that I am glad to support this measure because it indicates the setting up of a governmental body with some measure of power to go into the business of housing. I hope the day is not far distant when that measure of power will be increased and when the government of this country, in the name of the people, will give strong leadership and show real imagination toward the building of better homes for the Canadian people.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have heard with pleasure many young hon. members discuss the housing problem. In my opinion, they have done so most eloquently. Eloquence is a quite desirable talent, but it should not be forgotten that in speaking one must be not only eloquent but practical.
I know something about housing. In the town of Lachine twenty-five houses have been built and a loss of money has resulted. To-

Housing Act
day the government wants to do the same thing. Let me tell you that within ten years those houses will be offered for sale at ten per cent of their value. This means that in the end the people must always foot the bill. Workmen do not like to pay too much in taxes, but the government cannot make expenditures without levying taxes. They have to find money. There are people who earn $60 a week to whom I said "You are getting along well, since you have a good job." They replied "Yes, but we have to give everything to the government." A friend of mine has built an eight-unit apartment house. The cost to him has been $20,000 incliTding the lot. Each one of those apartments has four rooms and the rental is $25 a month. The eight apartments bring him $2,400 a year, that is twelve per cent on his investment. Out of this amount, of $2,400 he must provide for interest, insurance and upkeep, and pay municipal and school taxes.
All these expenses come to five per cent of his capital, which leaves him with a revenue of only seven per cent. If he entrusts the management of his property to an agent, he must pay him three per cent for collecting the rent alone, aside from the cost of repairs; by now, only four per cent remains. If he has not engaged an agent to look after the rent collection and the maintenance of his property, he himself must take those matters in hand. Indeed, he can make a success of his business only if he attends personally to his property. Yet, the man who has saved a small sum of money by his hard work naturally looks forward to a bit of a rest; he will do without it, however, if, the minute he sets foot in the house in the evening, his wife says: "In such and such an apartment upstairs, one of the doors will not shut. In another, there is something wrong with the plumbing and a pipe has sprung a leak." In other words, if this man does not entrust the management of his property to someone else, he is compelled, three or four nights a week, to do all the repair work. Moreover, he must collect the rent himself. When he calls on the tenants, a few may be unable to pay him, and he has to go back two or three times. I know something about it. As far as that man is concerned, where does he make his profit?
All the housing the government plans to build will cost the taxpayer a good deal of money. Green wood will be used, and ten years from now, the doors will not shut and the houses will sell at ten- per cent of their value. It is a problem which the authorities will find difficult to solve. It is an easy matter to talk about building when one does 47696-95i
not have to do it. Those who talk the loudest are those who are barely out of school. They are full of enthusiasm and they claim that they know everything but they know nothing.
I started working as a labourer when I was still a boy and I earned 25 cents per day; later when I had reached manhood I earned 10 cents per hour. I worked ten hours a day in order to earn one dollar. To-day a labourer earns $5 per day but he is no better off. The man who works 45 hours per week now wants a 40-hour week. Everyone knows that when a man works 10 hours a day his output is much greater than when he works but 40 hours a week. If men work fewer hours, they do less work and the goods cost more. Why is lumber so expensive to-day? In the old days, lumberjacks earned $20 per month; to-day I believe they earn $50. Then there is the hauling of the lumber to the railroad station and to the contractors' yards. All that costs money. Indeed, I believe that the dollar which I earned when I was working for 10 cents per hour was worth as much as the $5 which labourers earn to-day. And that is not all. When we earn little, we spend little. "In my youth, a glass of spruce beer cost 1 cent; to-day, beer sells for 5 cents or 10 cents, according to the size of the glass. Therefore, one might ask: Are working men better off to-day than they were in my younger days? Is the worker in a better financial situation now than in my time? I wonder. I am very favourably inclined toward the workers for they are really deserving. We owe them the street cars, the sewers, the buildings of all kinds which we enjoy: they have built them. I am anxious to take their interest, but they must be made to 'understand that the less they will work, the higher the cost' of living will climb and the less money they will have in the end.
In my time, bricklayers were getting from 40 cents to 50 cents an hour; to-day, they get $1.25. Lumber is not the only material that has gone up in price; the trend has been general, it is evident in plumbing and all other fields of construction. Everything contributes to the high cost of housing. Twenty-five dollars a month for a four-room house is dear enough for any worker. We must therefore find a formula making it possible to build homes at reasonable prices so that the worker may be able to pay his rent. Otherwise, he will have to leave the premises. Even if he is in a position to pay, the landlord will have no return whatever from the property unless the tenant is able to make small repairs himself in the evening, such as painting a veranda, fitting a door, changing a washer on
Housing Act

a, .water faucet, and so on. If, tire government is the builder, they certainly will not attend to such small repairs. I am sure the hon. Minister, of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) would not do it. Thus, you can get an idea of what the cost of such, an undertaking will be for the government. I am wondering what good may come of all this and I leave it to you.

Mr. ANTHONY HLYNKA (Vegreville)I:
Mr. Speaker, the government's proposal in this housing resolution is still a debt-finance proposal, and for that reason it is doomed to failure. The minister's scheme will fail to meet the needs of all those who need homes the most, simply because their incomes will not be sufficient to cover either the rent or the cost of these dwellings. The government, I believe, must undertake to subsidize house building if it is to be a success. There is no other way. I think the Edmonton Bulletin puts the case perhaps better than I have heard it put in the house. In an editorial in its issue of July 5, 1945, it has this to say on the subject of housing:	.
No one can afford to devote, it is calculated, more than one-fifth of his income to housing accommodation. This means that most Canadians, servicemen and civilians, must limit their monthly rent to between twenty and thirty dollars or else upset tlmir entire household economy.
It seems obvious, then, that the only answer to the pressing problem is adequate government ^subsidy.
: There are three essential factors in the matter <of government housing subsidy'.
First, speed is essential. Unless something on a sweeping scale is done immediately, hundreds of thousands of Canadians and certainly thousands of Edmontonians are going to be homeless next winter.	.
Second, adequacy is essential. There is no use half doing it. Enough money must be provided so that everybody in Canada may live in a decent home.	.
Third, beneficiaries under the housing subsidy must not be loaded with unpayable debt or unpayable rentals. Permanent bankruptcy is just as bad as homelessness. What is needed, then, is a plan that operates immediately, provides adequate funds to house everybody and supplies the money on a non-interest-bearing basis w'ith a loss if need be of some of the invested capital.
The Bank of Canada is the repository, created by parliament, of the national credit. The government should borrow money from the Bank of Canada, without interest, and devote it to the immediate construction of houses at low rentals.
This progressive Edmonton newspaper has championed low-rental housing and low-cost housing for many years, and for that reason I believe that I cannot improve on the wording or the clearness with which this paper states
[Mr. Bonnier.}
the case. I should therefore like to quote from another editorial which appeared in the Edmonton Bulletin of July 10, 1945:
The additional 300 war-time houses to be constructed in Edmonton this year for veterans, complete with basements and other permanent fixtures, will probably rent from $32 to $40 per month, it is announced. The temporary war-time houses, without basements and full-length chimneys, rent from $22 to $30 per month. No one, particularly a service man who deserves every possible comfort, should be asked to take his family into a primitive and uncompleted structure. At the same time the rent of the completed houses, running from $32 to $40 per month, is much too high. It is calculated that the cost of accommodation should never exceed 20 per cent of the individual's income. These rentals, then, can only upset the entire household economy of most of those who will have to live in them.
From another editorial which appeared in the same paper, dated July 31, 1945, I will quote only the last paragraph:
What is needed Is a low-cost modern house adapted to low rentals, because the returned man, like 80 per cent of other Canadians, can neither buy an expensive dwelling nor pay more than $18 to $25 per month rent for it. But under existing circumstances there is no such thing as a modern low-cost house. If houses are to be provided at rents the servicemen and most other Canadians can pay somebody must take a. loss on the building of them. And the only agency that can absorb this loss is the dominion government which represents all the people of Canada.
I should like to quote from another editorial which appeared in the same paper on August 14, 1945:
The lamentable failure of the National Housing Act to meet the actual home-building needs of discharged servicemen has been amply-proved in Edmonton and presumably throughout Canada. The failure emphasizes the extremely urgent need for another plan, financed on public money', which will provide for veterans the type o' accommodation they need at prices they can pay. . . .
The theory was that an equity of $400 would get a serviceman a loan of $3,600, which would enable him to build a home for $4,000. It does not work out that way. In practice, the serviceman requires a cash equity of at least $1,200 to $1,500. Even if he gets the full gratuity ot $1,800, which implies five years service in Europe, lie still has not enough to provide for furniture. No modern house can be built to-day for less than $5,000. To borrow $5,000 he must have $1,450. That leaves $350 for furniture in the unlikely event that he has the full $1,800 gratuity. The whole point is that the plan has. failed because modern low-rental homes can only be built to-day at a loss. Only the people-of Canada as a whole are capable of absorbing that loss. The sooner Mr. Ilsley decides on adequate subsidies, without regard to profits or returns, the sooner will a start be made towards solving the most vexatious problem facing Canada.

May I quote one more passage, from an editorial which appeared in the same paper on August 24, 1945:
In spite of the clear-headed statements of the Hon. C. D. Howe on the housing situation, that major problem still remains unsolved, because the circumlocution of debt finance has yet to be surmounted. The Hon. J. L. Ilsley clings to his obsolete bookkeeping system like grim death. Debt is still the incubus on house building. It should be possible to get desperately needed housing built just as desperately needed ships were built in Canadian yards during the war. Debt finance was set aside in the case of the ships. Debt finance will have to be set aside in the case of the houses.
I simply wish to emphasize the point that until and unless the government undertakes to subsidize housebuilding, our people will not have the homes in which to live, for the simple reason that the average Canadian does not receive an adequate income to enable him to purchase a home which would be comfortable for him'and his family, and by the same token a soldier who comes back from overseas and receives only his gratuity is not in a position to invest large sums of money in order to build a proper home. No one knows whether these men will obtain jobs which will bring them sufficient incomes to take care of their needs and at the same time to house their families.	.
Having made these suggestions, I maintain-that the minister and the government would be well advised to consider some scheme whereby the building of houses for individuals of limited means who desire them may be subsidized, and in that way necessary homes will be made available for our people.
I was not surprised that the group to my immediate right supported or showed their anxiety to support the measure because it appears to them that the government is going into house building. Anything which has the appearance of being state-controlled or state-owned would naturally be acceptable to them. They have taken the same attitude toward such measures as civil aviation. But so far as we of this group are concerned, we are never too anxious to give our unqualified support to any scheme, whether it appears to meet the situation or not, until and unless it is shown to us that it can be made financially possible, and until the government can indicate that the purchasing power in the hands of the average Canadian will be increased to purchase a home or rent a house at a reasonable cost. That is something that we of this group often repeat on the floor of the house, and there is no getting away from it. Unless the people of this nation have sufficient money with which to buy the things they need, whether it be housing or anything else, all
schemes that are brought forward will simply fail. We shall not have to wait very long to find that a great number of our returned men will be unable to pay the high rental costs that will be demanded of them,' because there is no guarantee that their incomes will be kept at a high level. Therefore, unless the government is willing to assure the Canadian people that everything possible will be done to keep that income at a high level, there is no chance that any scheme which is based upon debt finance will succeed. I again urge the government to consider this problem very seriously, because I believe that every Canadian is entitled to a home and that nothing should stand in the way of our people if they wish to build homes or to rent low-rental houses, provided that they are accommodated and their families are happy, so that we may have a happier and more satisfied nation.

DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
Before the committee proceeds to study the various items of the estimates, I wish to make some remarks of a general nature. I had not considered taking part in the present debate before hearing the speeches made by various members of this house. Since the estimates have been placed before the committee, I have listened carefully

Demobilization-Naval Services
to what has been said and I think I can summarize what has taken place so far as follows.
We have heard some hon. members criticize the government for not doing enough toward the formation of a peace-time navy, while on the other hand some others have considered that we are doing too much in the very same respect. I believe that the whole principle in medio stat virtue should apply in this case and that we can in all sincerity say, after having listened to the members of the house, that the government is just doing enough.
Of those who claim that we are not doing enough I must ask if they are prepared to admit that the government is not therefore spending enough. It is all very well to ask the government to have a large navy with a greater number of personnel and better ships, but in order to have such a navy we must be prepared to pay for it. No one wishes more than I do to see Canada with a large navy, a navy of such a size that full protection of our coasts, both east and west, shall be assured. However, we must not lose sight of the fact that our country is only a small nation and cannot spend forever as we did during the emergency that has existed in the last six years. It is difficult to understand hon. members who ask the government to provide a larger peace-time military establishment and yet do not hesitate at the same time to blame the same government for not cutting down the heavy taxes which our people must pay.
I always understood that the main reason for having opposition parties in parliament was to give to those in charge of the administration of the country the opportunity of receiving constructive criticism, which means the receiving of practical suggestions. I do not think this end has been achieved so far in this debate by our hon. friends on the other side of the house.
If Canada cannot afford a large navy we must therefore endeavour to look for quality since quantity is beyond our reach. How can we attain this maximum of quality in the formation of a peace-time navy without imposing too heavily on our budget? To my mind the first step to be taken toward this end is a careful selection of officers and men who are to form our peace-time personnel. At the present time our navy is being demobilized at an accelerated speed. In going through this demobilization period I hope that naval service headquarters will take into consideration first the qualifications of officers and men who wish to remain in the naval service. We must not forget that during the period of peace which followed the last great war we were too

much inclined to forget that Canada had a navy and, moreover, we did not pay enough attention to the fact that it might ever need one. It was only when war suddenly broke out in 1939 that we woke up to the fact that Canada had for all practical purposes almost no navy at all. We must not forget this historical moment in the history of our navy, when, at the outbreak of the conflict, the British admiralty wired our then chief of naval staff asking when Canada would be ready to send across the ocean the first convoy to the British isles. Less should we also forget the historical answer which was sent from naval service headquarters and which marked the beginning of the battle of the Atlantic by a single but brave word, " immediately.'-
I must here pause to pay high tribute to our then chief of naval staff for his courageous answer and also to those officers and men who did not hesitate to embark on our obsolete ships in order to deliver to our allies the badly needed goods. We have afterwards seen brave sons of this country go to sea for the first time in their lives, forgetting their lack of sea experience, but listening only to their brave hearts which were called to serve their country. Our losses were heavy, and Canada suffered a greater loss than that of ships and materials, because we then had to suffer the loss of some of the bravest men who ever lived on this continent.
I sincerely hope that this will never happen again, and the way to prevent it is to see that Canada keeps ready for any emergency which may occur in the future. That is why, as I have said previously, I hope that the nucleus of our peace-time navy will be based more on quality than on quantity of personnel to offset the disadvantages we had at the beginning of the war owing to the fact that we lacked trained personnel.
At the beginning of the conflict training establishments were rapidly opened throughout the country, and I must here pay another tribute to the personnel who taught in these training establishments at Halifax, Esquimalt, and later at Cornwallis, not mentioning our various reserve divisions all over Canada, which looked after preliminary training of recently recruited personnel.
After receiving, in a relatively short period, extensive training, our men were sent in ships where they acquired in actual warfare priceless sea experience for five or six years. In addition to preliminary training in gunnery, navigation, torpedo communication, and so forth, our training establishments were giving specialist courses which were of a very high standard. I must here mention in

Demobilization-Naval Services
particular the lung navigation course which was given in H.M.C.S. Kings under the direction of that hard-working officer, Commander Siverts. I myself had the great advantage of benefiting by the good work of that officer. The result of this training, combined with sea experience, contributed greatly to the fact that toward the end of hostilities we had a navy of qualified personnel. I do not hesitate to add that a single year of sea experience during the conflict which has just ended counts for more than three years of experience and training under peace-time conditions, no matter how highly trained is our peace-time personnel. That is why I say that in demobilizing our naval personnel we must do our best to keep within the ranks of our permanent force officers and men who have acquired experience during the war. How can we retain this personnel? This brings me to another consideration which must be taken into account during this demobilization period. That is, the consideration of the age of officers and men who are to be retained in the navy. We have had so far a lieutenant navy. Believe me, this was not due to the fact that top-ranking officers, in charge of the administration, voluntarily barred promotions, but rather due to the class of ships in which our officers were called to serve.
As everybody knows, the rank of a sea-going, officer goes with the class of ships in which he sails. We therefore have officers who have served for five or six years and now hold only the rank of lieutenants or acting lieutenant-commanders. If we do not give them an opportunity of seeing ahead of them a chance of rapid promotion so that their financial status may be compared with the standard of wages being offered at the present time to civilians, we consequently cannot expect these officers to be inclined to join our permanent force. On the other hand, if we do consider the question of age and give them the advantage of earning as much in the navy as they can expect to earn in civilian life, then we shall ipso facto interest them. The means to achieve this end is to set an average age for our permanent navy. I must add that the United States navy has followed this practice and has recently promoted a large number of its junior officers.
The third and last consideration which I suggest should be taken into account in the formation of a permanent navy is that of national representation. I believe that Canada and national unity will gain a great deal if the various racial groups in this country are proportionately represented in our permanent navy.
One has to serve his country to realize the deep love for it which beforehand might have lain dormant in his heart. If we see to it that our sons, no matter what racial groups they represent, serve together, we have every reason to hope then that these sons will become strongly attached to each other and will form the nucleus of a truly united nation, which we have for so long endeavoured to form in Canada.	-
Before closing these brief remarks, I must congratulate the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services (Mr. Abbott) upon having given the officers oi the Royal Canadian Navy, permanent and reserve personnel as well, the same distinctive stripes, and for having combined the R.C.N.R. and R.C.N.V.R. under a single reserve. This will eliminate, I think, this friction which has existed to a certain degree between permanent and reserve officers and even between the two former reserves and will, I hope, contribute to give Canada, if not a large, at least a united and strong peace-time navy.

I should like to ask the minister a question having to do with the manner in which the navy regards naval personnel who run afoul of civilian authority, something which quite often happens. We had a rather sad experience this summer in the Halifax riots, when a sailor found himself picked up by police. In the trial next day he found that certain evidence was given against him. I understand from the man that he had difficulty in finding someone to conduct his defence, because there appeared to be no one there who was authorized to plead his case for him.
This man understood the situation he was in, and thought the best thing to do was to plead guilty, and to take what he thought would be a fine of $50 or $100. He was surprised, however, when he found that, upon pleading guilty, he was sentenced to three years imprisonment. The man found himself in the predicament that he must try to appeal his case in order to get justice, and again he found the difficulty of getting the right kind of legal defence which would be afforded by an able lawyer. The man may be in such a position in regard to his own defence that he cannot afford a really first-class lawyer. The result has been that this man has lost his appeal, and now faces the reality of having to serve a three-year sentence, thereby bringing disgrace upon himself and his family, and losing all his gratuity. I believe that probably the only resource left to him is in the matter of remission, through the Minister of Justice.
How many cases are there where naval personnel arq sentenced and left in civilian gaols for civilian offences? How many cases are there where naval courts have sentenced men :o punishment, and where the punishment is *arried over and completed in civilian gaols? I have before me information put eut by the rehabilitation information committee of, I presume, the wartime information board. This information concerns naval discharge procedure, and it says that, first, a man is drafted to a discharge transit centre and, second, that he receives a complete physical examination in the following respects: medical, X-ray, dental and blood test. In talking to many naval men I have been informed that in connection with their medical

examination they are given X-rays of the chest, but no other X-rays are taken. There is no X-ray taken of their teeth. The naval dentists are all doing a good job, and the men say that they are good dentists, but are overworked. The hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat said that demobilization in the navy was being carried on at an accelerated speed. It is because of that accelerated speed of demobilization that the dentist, instead of X-raying the teeth of a man being discharged, takes his instruments, merely taps the teeth and if the man yells he puts down on the chart just what teeth need attention. When that man is discharged or sent home on leave he may go to his dentist to have his teeth checked up according to the chart given him by the naval dentist. He may have two, three or more teeth filled according to that chart, when he may have half a dozen or more abscesses under his teeth. I have known of cases where these naval men have had to pay out of their own pockets, not $5 or $10 but ten times that much in order to have their teeth taken out and a new set of star teeth, the kind that comes out at night, put in.
When men are discharged and given charts by the naval dentists they should be given a blank certificate good for a month or two after their discharge, so that if their teeth are defective by civilian dentists they can have them fixed up. X-rays should be taken"not only of the chest and lungs for T.B. spots, but of the whole body. I understand that blood tests are taken, but in some cases it is only a blood count and the blood is not tested for sugar or other purposes.
The third item is the rehabilitation lecture. I know some of these men have had this, but others have not. With this accelerated speed of demobilization many men do not get the proper attention in regard to rehabilitation.
The fourth item has reference to final discharge establishment. That is all right. If the man is entitled to discharge, he proceeds oc leave. If he has been a good man, he gets his leave; if he has not, he gets it in the neck.
The next item is the final medical examination. This examination is carried on just like sausages going through a sausage machine. The final examination is not a thorough one.
I do not get these complaints from just one man who has been discharged; I have had them from dozens of men.
The next item refers to the counsellor. When a man is discharged from the navy he asks if he can interview the Department of Veterans Affairs counsellor. I am not sure, but I believe these counsellors would b.e navy men to interview men being discharged from the naval forces. However, the men find that 47696-96
Demobilization-Naval Services
they must wait two, three or four weeks for an interview. They do not want to stick around that long; they want to be doing something. This should be checked up.	,
The ninth item is in regard to the discharge certificates, et cetera. The men are given clothing priority slips good for thirty days. Would it not be wise to extend these to sixty days? During the first month a boy may continue to wear his service clothes, at least for part time. Quite often many parties are given to him because he has just come out of the navy; people are glad to see him home, and sometimes the thirty days have elapsed before he realizes he has to have a suit of clothes.
While I am on my feet I should like to ask the minister if his department, like the United States government authorities, are going to experiment with the atomic bomb as it affects the navy. In the United States they are testing the effect of the atomic bomb upon targets in the water, and they are carrying on other tests to decide whether the present bombs used by the United States navy are as good as the atomic bomb. I should like to mention another matter which has been a sore subject with the men in the navy. It is in regard to men on shore at Halifax and Victoria. all Royal Navy men who did not salute on the streets of those two cities, and evidently the Royal Navy men were given similar orders to pick up our men in the same circumstances. Just before this committee adjourned on the 22nd instant the minister said that he would'answer the questions which had been asked by the hon. member for York West with reference to the Royal Canadian Naval College. Before he answers those questions I should like to say a word regarding the college, which is located at Royal Roads on Vancouver island. I do not believe it would be possible to find a better situation for that college. It has delightful surroundings and is situated on the strait of San Juan, where there are various types of water and where one can very easily pass out from the strait into the Pacific ocean. Near at hand there is a lagoon on which elementary training can be done. I was pleased that the minister was able to say that the college would continue at Royal Roads.
Other questions referred to the extension of that college and1 to whether there would be any change in policy. At the present time the college takes in approximately one hundred cadets, some thirty of whom are permitted to go into the Royal Canadian Navy each year, the rest going into the Royal Canadian Navy Reserve. While the college education deals partly with the training of a naval officer in the particular subjects required of him in the navy, it also gives him a basic education on broad general lines as well as on scientific lines. It provides a good education for the cadet whether upon graduation he goes into the Royal Canadian Navy or into the Royal Canadian Navy Reserve or into civil life, because the curriculum includes such subjects as English, French, history, mathematics, physics, chemistry, engineering, in addition to the more particularly naval subjects such as seamanship, navigation, gunnery and torpedo work. Thus they get a sound theoretical and practical knowledge, and that course as it has been to date has fitted the boy for whatever career he may desire to take up upon leaving the college. To those cadets who do not go into the Royal Canadian Navy upon graduation a certificate is issued which is recognized by a great many Canadian universities, and cadets who hold that certificate of graduation are permitted certain academic credits when entering a Canadian university.
I was hoping that there was no intention to change the policy so as to restrict this broad outlook which the graduates have been given

Demobilization-Naval Services
in the past, because I believe that their outlook should be at least as broad as that of the boy entering a university from the ordinary college and that the cadets' general cultural background should be at least as good as that of his contemporaries in the university to which he goes.
The Royal Canadian Naval College is administered by a board of governors but partly owing to war conditions, I suppose, the board has seldom been able to call to its meetings the commandant of the college or his chief instructor. I would rather like to compare that situation with the condition which existed at the Royal Military College at Kingston, where there is an advisory board composed not only of soldiers but also of educationalists representing either the universities or the educational authorities in the various provinces. Has the minister any plans for bringing closer together the instruction which is given in educational establishments other than that of the Royal Canadian Naval College, with the Royal Naval College itself? I hope that we are not going to have too much professional control of that college.
Since applications for entry to the college have to be in the hands of the naval secretary early in the year, I think of parents who are considering sending their boys to this college, and are anxious to know whether there will be any change in the policy, and also whether there will be any increase in the number of cadets to be taken into Royal Roads during the coming year. With the expansion of the navy .over the pre-war navy, one might hope that the opportunity will be given to more boys to attend what I believe is an educational establishment of which this country may well be proud.
