speechtext:
I said, our fine harbour. I had in mind one harbour in particular, but I might mention as well the other one in New Brunswick, the port of Saint John. We in Halifax particularly are perhaps navy conscious because we have been so closely identified with the war effort. During the very early days when some of my hon. friends who may say "hear, hear," were hardly conscious that there was a war going on we were actively engaged in war work in Nova Scotia. Well do I recall the time in July, 1940, when a number of members, irrespective of party affiliations, went on a trip to Halifax and saw that city in its war garb actively engaged in the war effort. I felt then that it was a fine thing to have those members come to Halifax and see what was taking place. It gave them an insight into what was going on in the naval and other branches of the defence forces. I often felt sorry that they could not make a similar trip in 1944 or 1945 to see the progress that had been made in fortifications, and the .splendid work that had been carried on by the navy and the other branches of the defence services. I bring this matter to the attention of the minister because I believe that greater use should be made of the facilities of H.M.C. dockyards at Halifax. We have a very fine plant there, well equipped and well able to handle all repairs necessary for the ships of the Canadian navy, and I suggest that greater use be made of the facilities provided in the machine shop, so that general repairs may be carried out there instead of being sent elsewhere. I also suggest that the floating dock, which it is proposed to do away with through the War Assets Corporation, be kept there and made use of by H.M.C. dockyards. At the present time it is used for general ship repairs, but it should be there particularly for the use of the navy.
I am now going to speak about a matter which I hesitate to bring up, but it is necessary to do so. It is in connection with the Bedford basin magazine. As all hon.-members know, we had an explosion there in 1917 which resulted in the loss of 1,600 lives, besides property damage. That was brought about by the collision of two ships which were in a place where only one should have been. With that in mind I brought to the attention of the Department of National Defence, at a

Demobilization-Naval Services
very early stage of this war, the fact that I was fearful of what might ensue should such a thing happen again. The people of Halifax in that vicinity were concerned about the magazine. They were wondering whether necessary precautions were being taken, whether proper safeguards were being maintained in the handling of explosives. This year, in the middle of the summer, we had an unfortunate explosion there which might have been very much more serious so far as loss of life was concerned. As it was, it was very serious in respect of property. To show that this was a matter of concern to the people of Halifax and to members particularly, I will place on file a letter that was written by me to the then minister of national defence, dated February 7, 1942; and I would ask the minister to note the date, because it was early in 1942, February 7 of that year:
Hear Mr. Ralston:
I am worried and disturbed in respeot to the manner in which ammunition and explosives are handled at Halifax. The information which I have received is to the effect that explosives are being brought by rail to Windsor Junction, switched to the Dartmouth branch and unloaded at Dartmouth pier, from where they are transported by scow or lighter to ships in the Bedford basin.
The Dartmouth pier, as you no doubt will remember, is located near the residential district of North Dartmouth, and while this in itself may not be a real hazard, the rehandling and the possibility of the scows or lighter being bumped or in collision going through the Narrows, is to me something that should be given most careful thought.
None of us would want to see a repetition of that awful catastrophe of 1917 when two ships met at a point where only one should have been.
Two suggestions have been offered. One is that a wharf should be constructed near the present magazine in Bedford basin. This, if 1 remember rightly, was under a protected cove just south of the track used by the magazine. The other suggestion was that the explosives should be routed through county harbour.
If you consider this important enough, would suggest that you might discuss same with the Minister of Munitions and Supply and the Minister for Naval Services.
I put that on the record so that the Minister of National Defence will know that it was brought to the attention of not only the then Minister of National Defence but of the Minister of Munitions and Supply, who advised me that the movement of ships came under the transport controller. I wrote to him somewhat along the same lines and I do not need to read that letter. Notwithstanding those representations made to the ministers, things were allowed to carry on in a manner, as stated in my letter, that gave grave concern to the people of Halifax.
I should now like to find out what steps have been taken and are being taken to prevent a recurrence of such an incident. I am not going to advocate, as certain bodies have done, doing away with the magazine. In my opinion, if we are to have a naval Atlantic base at Halifax, with ships coming in and going out, it is necessary that there should be a source of supply; but I say that every safeguard should be taken to prevent another accident such as that which we experienced just a few months ago.
I am now inquiring as to what steps have been taken with regard to an establishment such as they have in coastguard defence, or an establisment such as they have in the United States at the present time. A large number of men are being let out from the naval services and are anxious to continue their connection with the naval service. From the ranks of fishermen and those who have had experience in the navy I believe an efficient force could be formed w'hieh would be available in case of future need.
When the minister replies I should like him to advise us as to what steps, if any, are being taken in connection with the formation of an auxiliary branch such as I have mentioned. When the items are under consideration I propose to ask further questions with regard to certain expenditures. ,

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
The first question asked by the senior hon. member for Halifax relates to the steps taken to ensure so far as possible that there will not .be a recurrence of the unfortunate explosion which took place in the Bedford magazine. I covered that in part in my preliminary statement in introducing these estimates. There is no doubt that there was over-storage of ammunition at the Bedford magazine. The storage of ammunition, as it was in the open, was not safe and did contribute to the unfortunate explosion. The special committee which was set up under Colonel Ogilvie, in addition to the naval inquiry, has visited the magazine on two occasions. The damaged ammunition has now been largely removed. I think the area c&n now be taken as being safe so far as human precautions can make any magazine area safe. [DOT]
So far as the future is concerned, the quantity of ammunition stored in that magazine will be very much less than was the case during the war or was the case perhaps even prior to the war. The main ammunition stock, so far as the navy is concerned, will in future be stored at Renous which, as the committee knows, is in New Brunswick on the east coast, and Kamloops on the west coast.

I have not had an opportunity to study in detail the report which Colonel Ogilvie made a week or ten days ago, but substantially he has advised us that he is satisfied with the steps that are being taken to clear up the magazine area. He has made certain recommendations which are being implemented, and I think my hon. friend and the people of Halifax can rest assured that every measure is being taken to make sure that there will be no recurrence of the unfortunate explosion which took place last June.
With regard to the second question as to coastal defence with some type of fishermen's reserve, I am afraid I am not in a position to make any statement at the moment, but I shall take note of the suggestion and discuss it with the staff to see what their views may be as to the suggestion which my hon. friend has put forward.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
I think we are all in agreement that the Halifax naval explosion damages should be paid; the losses should be made good to those who suffered because of the explosion. I have a specific case on my desk of an indirect loss to a farmer in connection with this explosion. This farmer, who was a poultry raiser, shipped on the day before the explosion, 129 pounds of young chickens, broilers, to Halifax. He had them [DOT]on ice before shipment by express. The train was delayed because of the explosion, and the shipment was spoiled and was a complete loss so far as the producer was concerned.
He made a claim on the Canadian National Express, but they repudiated it, although they recognized the shipper's loss, inasmuch as the express company stated that they were not responsible for the delay and spoilage. This industrious farmer would like to know to whom he should apply for ledress with respect to this shipment. I understand that many or all the other claims have been recognized. The claim has not yet been filed because the shipper did not know to whom to submit the claim.
There is anothy matter to which I should like to refer. What is the policy of the minister or the government with respect to the loeation of the Royal Canadian Naval College, or such an institution for the Canadian naval services on the eastern coast? The Royal Canadian College was located on the eastern coast years ago. It was destroyed by another unfortunate explosion in 1917, to which the senior hon. member for Halifax has just referred. That college building and equipment were completely destroyed and not reestablished at the time. It has been felt in fMr. Abbott.]
Nova Scotia that that province is entitled to have the college located on the eastern Atlantic coast. While we are not envious of the Pacific coast, yet we do not want to be always the losers and have our establishments taken from us and be made to suffer for the benefit of other parts of Canada. I should like a statement from the minister as to the policy of the department with regard to the reestablishment of a naval college in Nova Scotia.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: As to the claim for the loss of chickens I can give my friend a free legal opinion on it, but perhaps I had better not do that-

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: It might not be worth very much.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
It would not be worth very much, no. As to where the claim should be made, E. L. Cousens, administrator of Atlantic ports, is in charge of adjusting claims resulting from the Bedford Basin explosion.
As to the sight of the Royal Canadian Naval College, the present location, as the committee knows, is Royal Roads on the west coast. It was established there during the war. What may be done in the future, I am not, of course, in a position to say at the moment, but I may say there is no immediate intention to move the college from its present location.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
I must tell the minister that his predecessor gave this house to understand that at least some part of the Royal Canadian Naval College would be reestablished on the Atlantic coast. That is the impression he gave me. I am surprised1 and disappointed that the minister would repudiate our claims in Nova Scotia at this time.
. I said a few moments ago that this is one more case where the eastern provinces are the losers for the benefit of central Canada, the prairies and the Pacific coast. In this case it is to British Columbia. I believe the Atlantic coast is entitled to the reestablishment of this naval college. If there is to be only one such college it should be reestablished in Halifax and not on the Pacific coast. If reestablished in Halifax, on the Atlantic coast, it would be in close contact with naval ships, and other institutions of Great Britain, and they could work together in harmony, one for the benefit of the other. I repeat that we in the east, as a matter of right, are entitled to that. It was lost to us because of an unfortunate explosion,' and I say that the college should be reestablished in Halifax. The people of Nova Scotia will resent deeply the minister's refusal at this time to give an assurance that the Royal Canadian Naval College will be reestablished on the Atlantic coast.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: I was not aware that my predecessor, Mr. Macdonald, had given the undertaking to which the hon. member for Cumberland has just referred. In fact my information is that he did not give such an undertaking; but no doubt the hon. member can give me the reference in Hansard, or wherever it was recorded. I have nothing to add to the statement I made a minute ago.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: It was not my intention to speak about the navy, but at the last moment, and for several very good reasons, I decided to say a few words. I have noticed that in this debate there has been considerable men-_ tion of recruiting for the Royal Canadian Navy, and it has been pointed out that it is the intention of the government to maintain a peace-time navy of considerable proportions. A good many members have been wondering why we now find difficulty in getting recruits for the navy.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: We are not.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: As one who has had experience in the navy, I propose to tell the committee why we are having difficulty in obtaining those much needed sailors.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
But we are not having
difficulty, if I may interrupt my hon. friend.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Well, several hon. members have been expressing a doubt.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Yes, but perhaps I have better information than some others have.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: I accept the minister's statement that he has sufficient sailors to man the navy. But I think all hon. members will be willing to agree that a number who have spoken in the last few days have stated that there has been difficulty in obtaining sufficient men to enlist in the navy.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Reconstruction
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: But they were wrong.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
I wish to state first that I am not blaming the government on this point. The reason why men do not wish to serve in the navy is that service in that branch of the armed forces is particularly hard. It is especially hard in the Royal Canadian Navy, not because of anything the government has done to make it hard and, I might say, not because of anything the government could do to make it better. It is on account of the fact that we have a navy of small ships. I think all sailors will be willing to agree that service on small ships is quite difficult, and it is difficult because of extremely cramped conditions. When one starts out on a ship he finds plenty of food; the ship is clean and,
generally speaking, conditions are satisfactory. But before he approaches the end of that trip the food is almost gone; one is living on short rations and under conditions which could be described as anything but favourable.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: To what size of ship is the hon. member referring?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
To the chief kind of ship used by the Royal Canadian Navy for escort duty during the last war, namely corvettes. I believe I am correctly stating the facts when I say that the corvettes were the chief escort vessel.
To go on from that point, I wish to repeat that we are not blaming the government for that condition. But after three or four years of service on such ships men do get tired of going to sea. I venture to say that when peace was declared many Canadian sailors fondly looked forward to the day when they would get out. of the Royal Canadian Navy.
I am not saying that everyone holds that view, because I have met a number of men who are willing to continue to serve with the navy. But the majority of them wish to get home. If we do have difficulty in maintaining our navy I suggest that we might compensate the men for those hard living conditions by increasing the pay of the lower ranks. For instance, an able seaman or a second-class stoker starts out at a pay of $1.25 or SI-35 a day. It may be $1.50; I am not sure, but it is around there somewhere, and it is difficult to get higher pay. It takes considerable time to work up to, let us say, a seaman petty officer, where there would be a considerable increase in the rate of pay. I would suggest that the rates for the men in the lower classifications should be raised to the point where their remuneration would be similar to what they would get for peace-time work.
I -would suggest, further, that we do something to remove tradition from the Royal Canadian Navy. I think we have reached the time when we must realize that Nelson is dead. I do not say that in any derogatory sense, but the view held by many sailors on the ships of the Royal Canadian Navy is that things are done in the way Nelson did them. In the Royal Navy it is quite common to hear them say that they are doing things in the way Nelson did them.
Another improvement we might make would effect what one might term the officer class. I think it is correct to say that there was a greater difference between the living and pay conditions of the officer and rating classes in the navy than there was between the officer and ordinary soldier classes in the
Demobilization-Naval Services

army. We have reached the point where men, especially those in the Royal Canadian Navy, feel keenly that they are an inferior lot, so far as their positions in the navy are concerned. I realize fully that we must have discipline in the navy1, but I think it would be quite possible to meet the suggestion I have made while at the same time maintaining efficiency.
I have only one more statement to make, namely, that the minister ought to remind the brass hats in the navy, if I may so describe them, that Nelson is dead, and that the Canadian navy should be reconstructed along modem lines.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
I am sure the hon. member for Churchill has not overstated the hardships of serving in small ships. I know, too, that he speaks from personal experience, something which only very few in the house can do. I simply wish to point out, however, that I hope in the future service in the navy will be in somewhat larger and very much more modem ships. As I indicated in my statement, the post-war navy will consist of two light cruisers of the most modern design, up-to-date destroyers and two large aircraft carriers. At least those two carriers will be the largest we have had in the Royal Canadian Navy. Therefore I say that the man who stays on in the navy may look forward to conditions very much better than those described by the hon. member for Churchill.
I will bring his remarks about Nelson's death to the attention of the staff.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
Speaking in the house
on October 22, as reported at page 13S5 of Hansard, I said to the minister:
If the minister desires to get his estimates through, as he no doubt does, there must be complete frankness on his part with the members of the house.
Later on in the debate the minister gave a promise to me that he would make a statement to-night. When he is asked to make the statement, he says he would prefer not to make it.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Just one moment; I rise to a point of order. I have not refused to make a statement. I did not say to my hon. friend I would make it to-night. I told my hon. friend I would be glad to make a statement with respect to the Carr charges. I shall be glad to make that statement, but I want him to repeat the charges from his place in the house under the proper items and I will answer every one.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
You did not ask that the
other night.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
Whether I asked it the
other night or not, I am asking it to-night.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
That is all right, but
there was one question I asked the minister, and that was not a question of making charges. I asked the minister if he would let the house know who the Acadia Construction Company was. That company was born since the beginning of the war and has done possibly the greater amount of naval construction work done in the maritimes. That is information we should have. That is not a charge.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
I shall be very glad to
answer my hon. friend. The Acadia Construction Company comes under the Minister of Munitions and Supply. As the hon. member knows or should know-he has been out of the house for some time-the Department of Munitions and Supply is the department of government which lets these contracts. So far as I am concerned or so far as my knowledge as Minister of National Defence for Naval Services is concerned, the Acadia Construction Company Is the contractor with whom the Department of Munitions and Supply has made a contract for work to be done at Shelburne, Nova Scotia, and elsewhere.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
You must have the
information.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
I shall take only a minute to refer to the comment made by the hon. member for Nanaimo about naval education, which the minister has already answered in part. The hon. member for Nanaimo expressed the hope that naval education would be conducted on a broad basis, and to my way of thinking that is a matter of great importance. It seem? to me there is only one thing we can say wdth confidence in looking forward to the future of military and naval and air operations, namely, that all kinds of new and unexpected things will arise. Our method of education should be very flexible. If the men are given merely technical education, that technique may pass away in two or three years. I was glad to hear the minister say that the matter was being carefully considered, but I would earnestly suggest to him that this education of our naval officers be carried on in the broadest way possible.
If we look back to the various climacterics of the war, to the crucial times, I suppose we will all agree that the battle of Britain in the late summer and early autumn of 1940-was the most critical of all. I think it can be said that we won that battle, not primarily because our airmen were braver or more skilful in the air. but because for years the air force had put forward great intellectual efforts in train-

Demobilization

Naval Services
ing their men. We were intellectually superior to the Germans in the air, and therefore we were able to win with smaller numbers. This question of military, naval and air education for the future is a matter of tremendous importance, and I hope the questions raised by the hon. member for Nanaimo will be dealt with in a thoughtful and not in an easy-going or perfunctory manner.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
The matter which I should like to bring to the attention of the minister follows somewhat along the line of the remarks of the last speaker. I wish to speak for a moment about what are commonly known as sea cadets. I do not know where that is covered specifically in this list, but I think it would come under either item 1 or item 2. I shall not be able to tell that until the minister has answered my questions.
When the naval estimates were last being debated, both the minister and the hon. member for Yale spoke about sea cadets. I should like to obtain some information about this work and about the remuneration of the instructors. The hon. member for Y'ale and the minister stated that the sea cadets were now recognized as being a most efficient body. I think it was the former who made it quite plain that the government should come to its support. The hon. member referred to the grave difficulties there were to keep this corps going. The very fact that he felt that would indicate that he considered that the government had not been supporting it very strongly.
Is it the fact that the air cadets and the army cadets are financed by the government while the sea cadets are not? The minister told us that he had a son in the sea cadets. I presume the minister contributes voluntarily to the navy league, but at the same time as a taxpayer he would be compelled to pay taxes to provide for the training of air cadets and army cadets. That does not appear to be an equitable situation.
Many of these instructors are teachers in the collegiate institutes. I understand that the air and army instructors are paid and are provided with uniforms and certain items of equipment. To my knowledge, several teachers in the high school system, because of -internal administration of the schools, were asked to transfer from the army or air cadets to sea cadet work. In a spirit of cooperation and patriotism, engendered I suppose by the necessities of war, they complied with that request, only to find themselves in the unfortunate position from a material point of view of not receiving like pay, as a matter of fact being actually out of pocket in the matter of at least some part of their uniforms.
I should like to hear the comments of the minister on this situation, particularly as to whether this condition is to be perpetuated in peace time. I would again refer to the remarks made to-night as well as those made by the minister himself as to the necessity of keeping up the fine work which has been done in this branch of naval education.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: I realize that a great deal of money has been spent on this branch of the work, but I have not had an answer to my question. Is it a fact that the man who gives his time to the training of sea cadets must suffer a pecuniary loss, or at least receives no pay for such work, when the army or air cadet instructor does? At least he is not paid for such work as the army instructor is. He has to provide himself with some part of his uniform, while the other has it provided for him. That is the point I wanted to bring out.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: I cannot say whether he does it at a financial loss or not. He is paid something, but whether it is comparable with what his opposite number receives who is training air force cadets or army cadets, I do not know, but I can make inquiries and try to get the information.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: The minister says that he is paid something. By whom is it paid?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: That is my information.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
The sea cadet officer will receive a clothing allowance, I believe, of something over a hundred dollars. That is to say, so much is allowed per corps, and where the corps has more officers than its complement, the amount would be reduced for each officer. So far as pay and allowances are concerned, when a sea cadet officer attends camp or a regular training period he is paid, and he is also paid his transportation; but so far as the regular weekly training is concerned, I have never met a sea cadet officer
Demobilization-Naval Services

-and I am interested in this movement- who cared very much whether or not he received remuneration. He was in it because he liked it, and remuneration was a secondary consideration. I believe, however, that the naval service are contemplating some relief in that respect, but I have never yet met a sea cadet officer who worried very much about the pay he was getting.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Perhaps I should have added that the whole cadet question is under consideration. I might point out to the committee that this year's appropriation for sea cadets is about $600,000, approximately the same as was spent last year. I do not need to tell the committee that expenditures in these days have to be carefully scrutinized. We are being urged 'to reduce taxes, and we have to be sure that the money we spend is spent in the best possible way. I think what my hon. friend the member for Wentworth has said is true, that the great majority of sea cadet officers are glad to render this service without remuneration, and, if so, that is something which should be done on that basis. But I will give the matter further consideration.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
I think the minister is unduly optimistic in thinking that he will get sufficient ratings to fill up the ranks of the permanent navy, and I was surprised to hear the minister's statement in reply to the hon. member for Churchill a few moments ago in view of the information contained in a return that was tabled in the house yesterday in answer to questions asked on October 18, when I asked:
1.	How many officers and ratings were actually enrolled in the permanent force of the Royal Canadian navy as of August 1, 1945?
2.	Of the ratings, how many comprised the seamen?
3.	How does this latter total break down as between chief petty officers, petty officers, leading seamen, able seamen and ordinary seamen?
4.	How many in each of these categories were enrolled in the permanent navy on August 1, 1939?
The return gives the number of able seamen in 1945 as 323, and in 1939, 359, or a reduction. The reduction in the ranks of ordinary seamen is greater, there being 268 ordinary seamen in 1945 as compared with 307 in 1939. These figures certainly do not seem to indicate that the ratings have been joining the permanent navy in any considerable numbers. As a matter of fact, our position so far as the last two categories I have mentioned is concerned is worse than it was in August, 1945.
I have had conversations with many young men out of the navy and with some still in it, and so far as the ratings were concerned I gained the definite impression that the service
[Mr. L- nnarrl.l
was not very popular with them, chiefly because they were subjected to a large number of petty annoyances which, as one of them expressed it were like a series of pin-pricks which eventually completely destroyed the very considerable enthusiasm with which he had joined the navy. I think that if anything like the 19,000 men required for our permanent navy are to be secured it will probably be essential to do away with a lot of the customs and traditions going back, as was said by the hon. member for Churchill, to the days of Nelson. No doubt they served a very useful purpose at that time, but many of them have ceased to serve a useful purpose to-day and serve only to irritate and discourage the ratings who are subjected to them. That must be coupled, I think, with an increase in pay to attract the men, which the minister spoke of the other day. This matter of old customs in the navy and petty annoyances apparently is a real grievance, and I would ask the minister whether any steps are being taken to remove these petty annoyances in order to make the service more attractive.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: I cannot answer that unless I know what the petty annoyances are. If my hon. friend *were to enumerate them I certainly could make inquiries and see what is being done to remove them. I would remind my hon. friend that ninety per cent of the officers in the permanent force are volunteers. I do not know whether my hon. friend was in his seat when I gave figures earlier to-day of enlistments in the interim force. The figure was 1,181, of whom 673 were ratings.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: If the minister would like a list I think I could supply it readily in the course of a day or two.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Perhaps my hon. friend would give one or two examples now.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: One example is in connection with the method adopted when men go on shore leave. Whether a man is in a ship or in barracks, apparently when he has an evening off he has to wait for the so-called "boat" before he can go, and if he misses one mythical boat he has to wait for [DOT] the next one, which may be an hour, or something else. I was told by two of these chaps that that was considered an annoyance. They were ready to go out for the evening but had to wait until the next mythical boat sailed.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
I wish to bring something before the minister for naval services, supplementing what was said by my colleague the hon. member for Saskatoon City a few

Demobilization-Naval Services
moments ago. He drew attention to the fact that there was a lack of uniformity in the treatment of cadet instructors in the three branches of the service, and he was rather facetiously, I fear, put aside on the plea that teachers are serving as volunteers from a proper sense of public spirit. Having been a teacher myself, I know we have had to volunteer to do thousands of things without remuneration from a sense of public spirit. Teachers generally are brought up to do just that. But if there is one form of treatment for airforce cadet instructors, another for the navy and another for the army, I think we should bring them all into line, so that there would not be the urge of cupidity among these instructors which might make them want to jump from one service to another because a uniform was provided in the one case and they had to contribute in the other.
Further to that, I have here a copy of the Canada Gazette of September 29 of this year, containing naval order No. 5216, which states, under the heading, "Grant in lieu of leave on discharge", certain procedures to be followed for discharging Canadian Wrens from the service. I quote:
(1) Payment of the grant in lieu of leave shall be confined to:
(a)	those personnel who, in the opinion pf the commanding officer, will bo assisted in their rehabilitation by immediate discharge prior to completion of leave, and
(b)	those personnel who are discharged to care of the Department of Veterans Affairs and. as a result, are prevented from proceeding on leave prior to discharge.
It also states that in such circumstances the grant will be approved without application in all cases when such personnel are unable to take leave due on discharge by reason of discharge to care of the Department of Veterans Affairs, and that the grant is to bp considered as a right for these personnel. Also it sets a cut-off date for the payment of this particular grant in lieu of leave as starting subsequently to the 19th April, 1945. The question I wish to direct to the minister with respect to this is, is this regulation, which is here applicable to the Wrens, uniform throughout all three services; that is, it may be that is generally applicable to the navy, but is it also applicable to the army and to the air force; and, if so, since when has that been applicable; because I know of cases of army personnel who were returned to Canada at the request of the Department of Veterans Affairs and who had to assume duties immediately upon discharge without having the privilege of disembarkation leave in Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: The answer is in the affirmative.' The same rule applies to all three services, and from the same date, and it was put in to meet just such cases as those to which my hon. friend has referred. After April 19, in most cases, in the discretion of the department, the rating or the officer or man, as the case may be, can be paid the pay for the thirty days leave in lieu of the leave.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: May I ask why this should have been cut off at April 19, when these officers and other persons who were called back to assist to set up the rehabilitation section of the Department of Veterans Affairs last December did not receive the same consideration?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
The answer to that is that, so far as officials in my department are aware, that was about the time the question first arose; and it was put through fairly promptly.
While I am on my feet, the hon. member for Cumberland is no longer in his seat, but I think I should point out what my predecessor. Hon. Angus L. Macdonald, said with respect to this naval college situation. It will be found in Hansard of April 4, 1945, at page 443:
As I indicated last night, while it may not be possible to establish two naval colleges in the country, and it may be that the naval college will continue in British Columbia, 1 would hope that there will be sufficient other naval activities in Nova Scotia more than to compensate for the loss of this educational institution. Nova Scotia has a great many educational institutions and perhaps we should operate this one in some other place.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: The hon. member for Calgary East mentioned petty grievances. A grievance that at least some men have is that in the rules and regulations as laid down, if a man appears with a button undone or his shoes not shined, the captain or any of the officers can say, "You will have ten days in the brig". It is too much; it is too severe, and that is what the men object to, little things like that. The rules and regulations should be changed, and our Canadian navy should have a manual of its own. I do not know whether what we use now is the 1936-37 or the 1926-27' British manual.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
Edited by Lord
Nelson.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
Well, Nelson would
know.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
I believe the United States manual is kept right up to date. It is modem; it is stream-lined, and we should have one as much up to date.
Demobilization-Naval Services

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
My hon. friend is a little
behind the times in his criticism, because the -new Naval Act came into force on October 15. We have a new stream-lined act, Canadian from stem to stem.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
I congratulate the minister
on that, because I have been after the navy department for the last five years, and eventually it has come round to thinking the way I do.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
Could the minister tell
us when we may expect, a decision regarding the policy for Royal Roads, because applications for next year have to be in early in the coming year? I am getting letters frequently from parents asking for this information.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
I realize it is important
that an announcement should be made as soon as possible, but I cannot give any more definite undertaking than I did a few moments ago. I assure my hon. friend that it is under the most active consideration-to use the popular phrase-and I think I should be in a position to make an announcement very soon.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Just one more question and I am through. Have men serving in Newfoundland any priority for the civil service; are they classed with men overseas? I understand from the minister for air that in regard to his branch of the service there is some move to take Newfoundland in, and I wondered whether the navy would also provide for priority with regard to jobs in the civil service.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
No, there is no such
priority, unless they were serving afloat. I understand that the whole question is being considered by the veterans committee. I have not been able so far to attend the meetings of the committee, but that is my understanding.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
I hope, with all this
urge for modernity and break with tradition, that the navy will not do away with the time-honoured custom of splicing the main brace.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
I think it may be taken
for granted that that custom will not be abandoned. Personally, like my hon. friend, I hope that it will not.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
On Monday evening the
minister dealt in reply to questions with the policy as regards the interim army. Over the week-end a young non-commissioned officer with an excellent war record covering five years came to see me. Will these boys

have to be attested, or will they continue under present attestation papers, or have any instructions been sent out to the various commands across Canada as to how to deal with these boys who wish to stay in the interim army?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: These are the naval estimates that we are on now. I may say that the same regulations apply, subject to necessary differences, to all three services. Perhaps I can answer my hon. friend by saying that, broadly speaking, the conditions in all three services so far as interim service is concerned are the same. Applications are being received in all three services by hostilities only personnel to continue their service up to September 30, 1947, on the conditions I outlined in some detail in my statement with regard to the army estimates. I do not know what particular form they fill out. I cannot say at the moment whether they sign a form, but I assume they do. I assume they must sign an enlistment form undertaking to serve until September 30, 1947, if accepted for that period. I made *an announcement in my army statement that if, when the terms of enlistment in the permanent forces are announced, they do not wish to avail themselves of the right to enter these forces they will be relieved of their undertaking to serve until September 30, 1947. Does that answer my hon. friend's question?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Yes, but there is one matter to which the minister has not referred. He has made reference to the two fine aircraft carriers. Is he aware that at No. 31 Collins Bay the fleet air arm, in the course of four years, has trained over 100 classes, averaging fifty to a class, making 5,000 in all? I did not hear him mention that.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
When I was discussing that matter, in answer to questions put by the hon. member for Yale, I said that the matter of training for the fleet air arm was now the subject of discussion between the air force and the navy. I indicated that in all probability, although I did not know-in fact I know it has .not been definitely settled-an arrangement would be made with the air force to utilize jointly bases on the east coast and the west coast. There are a considerable number of Canadians now fully trained as fleet air arm pilots and we anticipate that a good many of these will continue in the service; but of course in the future it will be necessary to provide for the training of further personnel. I cannot say now, however, where that training will be carried out, although I can say I am sure it will be carried out in conjunction with the air force R.C.A.F. training stations.

Demobilization-Naval Services

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Is the matter under the minister's department?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: It is a joint use of bases.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, are we engaged in a general discussion, or are we on item 1?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Before you decide that, Mr. Chairman, may I just be allowed to say a word about the fleet air arm. It arises out of a number of letters I have written to the minister about the position of Canadians who happen to be in the British fleet air arm. A number of Canadians have been in the British fleet air arm, and apparently they are receiving British rates of pay and are under British naval authority for discipline, discharge and so on. Could the minister make a statement to clarify the anomaly of these Canadians serving with the British fleet air arm?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: There are a considerable number of young Canadians enlisted directly by the Royal Navy for service in the fleet air arm. I know that to be the case because I have a young cousin serving with the Royal Navy now in the fleet air arm, and my understanding is that these Canadians joined the Royal Navy-not the Royal Canadian Navy but the Royal Navy-subject to the terms and conditions which were offered to them by that force. We have also a number of Royal Canadian Naval Volunteer Reserve chaps serving with officers who are serving with the Royal Navy on carriers for training purposes. But my hon. friend's question, I take it, had reference exclusively to Canadians who are serving with the Royal Navy and on the strength of the Royal Navy.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Yes. What machinery is there; what liaison has the Canadian government with the United Kingdom government for discharge? I ask the question because I have received a number of letters from these fellows, and' I believe that some of them enlisted in the R.C.A.F. and then transferred to the British fleet air arm.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: The Canadian government has no arrangement at all. They enlisted in the Royal Navy, made their contract with the Royal Navy, and that is the position they are in. My understanding is this-this is only hearsay, being the result of a letter I received from this young relative of whom I have spoken of-that he is being given the option of staying on with the Royal Navy, fleet air arm, or of obtaining transfer to the Canadian navy if that is available, or of getting discharge, but I cannot say that is generally applicable. Apparently that is the position in his case.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: It seems to me, Mr. Chairman, that if we are to get anywhere we might as well get down to the individual items before us. Every one of the questions asked in the last two or three hours could easily be asked on the particular items which appear on the list, and I think it is about time we discontinued the general discussion.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: I thank the hon. member for his suggestion. We have nearly reached the question stage, all the speeches and remarks on general topics having apparently been pretty well exhausted. I would therefore welcome an effort to proceed with the items one by one.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Those of us who would stay with the item are being robbed of an opportunity of discussing particular questions later on, because we shall be told that the item has already been disposed of.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: We have not passed any yet.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: I realize that, and that is why I suggest that it is about time we got down to the individual items.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: The point raised by the hon. member for Camrose (Mr. Marshall) is well taken. If I recall correctly, it was agreed that under item 1, which we have been discussing, there would be allowed a more or less general discussion. As the hon. member has said, we have had a very wide general discussion and it should now be possible for the committee to carry item 1.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: No, Mr. Chairman, we have not yet discussed item 1. Item 1 states definitely civil salaries, and we have not been discussing civil salaries this evening.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: May I interrupt again to suggest that the committee confine further discussion to item 1, civil salaries and wages.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Item 1 has not yet been called.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Shall I call item 1 now?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Mr. Chairman-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: The hon. member for Camrose has the floor unless the committee wishes me to call item 1. Before I call item 1, however, the hon. member for Wentworth (Mr. Lennard) would like to say something.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
The minister and the hon. member for Yale, earlier in the debate the
Demobilization-Naval Services

other evening, mentioned in a kindly way the Royal Canadian Sea Cadet Corps, and in view of the remarks made by the hon. member for Yale, I should not like the impression to go out that the Royal Canadian Sea Cadet -Corps were principally being maintained as a recruiting agency for the Royal Canadian Navy, because, while basic training, seamanship and communications are thorough-these boys receive a thorough training-nevertheless the Royal Canadian Sea Cadet Corps have a fine reputation as a youth movement in Canada. They are doing a great deal of good work in character building. They are perhaps one of the greatest deterrents of juvenile delinquency in our congested areas. I wanted to make that point clear and to tie it in at this time with the estimates.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: I quite agree with all that the hon. member for Wentworth has said.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: On a couple of occasions I wanted to ask a question along this line, but I deferred it because I thought it came under some other minister. The reply given by the minister to the question asked by the hon. member for West York is not correct so far as I understand it. Most of these young men who enlisted in Toronto were taken right out of the schools by the Royal Air Force.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: That is something completely different from what I was talking about. I am speaking of young aviators who were enlisted here by the Royal Navy, not by the R.A.F. They served in the Royal Navy as part of the fleet air arm. I know that because that was exactly what happened to a young cousin of mine. It was not the Royal Air Force; it was the Royal Navy, and he w'as in Royal Navy uniform before he left Canada.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
I was wrong in designating the particular air force. It is the fleet air arm to which I had reference. They were enlisted right out of schools in Toronto. They were boys of seventeen to eighteen years of. age-. After considerable training they finally arrived at Pensacola, after going over to England and coming back again. I myself know of a number who made application by request at Pensacola to transfer, I presume to join the Canadian service. Later on, these ooys were scattered all over. Some of them finally arrived in the Pacific. Those who arrived in the Pacific and in the Indian ocean are the ones I have in mind. Others who did not get that far were gotten in touch with by the authorities who accepted their applications for the Canadian service. The other 
lads who were out in the Pacific and Indian ocean were too far away for the authorities to make contact with them and apparently their applications have not been accepted. What I wish to know is, are the applications that they put in at Pensacola still open to acceptance by the department? '

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: I shall have to look into that to make sure. I think I can answer it by saying that unless they are willing and anxious to continue to serve, at least on an interim basis, they will not be accepted, because we are now taking enlistment transfers only of those who wish to serve in the post-war navy. We are having, of course, no more hostilities only transfers, as we had it up to the end of the war; but I shall make some special inquiries about the case.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Does the matter come under the minister?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: It would come under me if they want to transfer to the Royal Canadian Navy. If they want to transfer to the Royal Canadian Air Force, of course it would come under my colleague, the Minister of National Defence for Air.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: I wish to know what is to happen to these young lads?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: I can answer that only in this way, that they are not on the strength of the Canadian army, navy or air force. If they apply for transfer to one of these forces there would be two factors involved: first, whether the Royal Navy would be willing to release them; and, second, whether the Royal Canadian Navy would be willing to take them. But I am answering the second question in this way: I do not think the Royal Canadian Navy would want to take them on unless they want to serve in our permanent force up until September 30, 1947.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
The minister apparently
has not the facts because there is a number who have been taken on.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
Apparently not after the
war. We were taking them up to the end of the war. We were taking what I referred to for brevity as hostilities only transfers. We would only take them in that case. Hostilities are over, and we are starting to build a permanent post-war force.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
As I see it, un^gss you
treat them all the same you will treat some of them unfairly. All the boys that I have in mind made application at Pensacola, but afterwards got scattered too far away to be in contact with our officials here.

Demobilization-Naval Services

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
I do not know how many
are involved. There may be far too many to come into the Canadian force. However, I shall make some further inquiries.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
What item are we on,
Mr. Chairman?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
I understand we are
now on item 1, "civil salaries."

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
According to the auditor general's report for 1943-44 an amount approximating $5,800,000 was spent and the number of civilian employees was 10,384. The hon. member for York South asked the minister last night the number of civilian employees there were for 1944-45. The minister was unable to give the figures, but he gave the figure to the end of September of this year as 4,240. In other words, there is somewhere a decrease of around 6,000 in the civilian employees, and yet we find that actual expenditures for civil salaries during the last year were $7,352,832, or a decided increase.
There is another matter I should like to draw to the attention of the minister. The actual estimate last year was $6,500,000, whereas the actual expenditures-and the only things We should deal with now are realities, not estimates-for last year were $7,352,000, or an increase from the estimate to actual expenditures of somewhere in the neighbourhood of $840,000. In the light of the fact that from 1943-44 to the present time it is evident that the number of civilian employees has been greatly decreasing, will the minister tell us that the decrease to the end of September was
4,000	civilians?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: I do not know; I have not seen the auditor general's report to which my hon. friend is referring, but I think he must be including the civilian employees in all the armed services.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: No, I am not; you will pardon me. For the minister's benefit I may tell him that what I am reading from is headed: "Department of National Defence- Naval Services, civil salaries and wages, $5,827,669.45." Then it goes on to say, "As of March 31, 1944, there were 10,384 civilian employees paid from this account." It has nothing to do with the army or the air force. The minister should give a clear and detailed statement as to the civilian employees and the amounts spent for this item during the last two years.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext:
Perhaps I can clear that up very quickly. The salaries included in this item are only civil servants properly so-called. In addition, under item 10, "acquisition, construction, charter, repairs and upkeep of ships,"
there appears the very large sum of $50,000,-
000.	There is a substantial amount in there for civilian employees, because in the repairs of ships at various points there is a considerable number of civilian workers employed, as well as those who are on salary.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: I realize that distinctly. If the minister will get the public accounts for 1943-44 he will see that there is a separate item which compares with the items as now set forth in these estimates. He will find an item exactly the same in the old auditor general's report.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: I cannot explain it at the moment. The figures which are given me show the number of civilian employees carried in 1944 when the estimates were prepared, the year my hon. friend is talking about; 4,798, that is a figure I did not have the other night when the hon. member for York South asked me the question too. The present number is 4,240.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I am willing to allow the item-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: It is eleven o'clock.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: -to go through, if the minister will give me an assurance that he will give me the figures to-morrow.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: I will certainly look into the figures. I question whether the committee is ready to allow the item to go through. I shall be delighted if they are.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: We might think up . another question.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Does item 1 carry?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: No.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR NAVAL SERVICES
speechtext: Carried.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Progress reported.
It being five minutes after eleven o'clock, the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
Friday, October 26, 1945.
